The story of Black Mountain College (BMC) has grown to mythical
proportions since the liberal arts school officially closed its doors in
1957. Countless books, exhibitions, and artworks have been created
to capture what it was like to live and learn at this singular college
and to chart its unparalleled cultural legacy. But before this book,
nobody had written about the farm at BMC in any great detail.
Nestled in the breathtaking Appalachian Mountains of
Western North Carolina, Black Mountain College was a beacon of
experimental art practice and communal living in America. Against
the odds, the school was founded with limited financial resources
during the Great Depression and, over the years, it became one of
the most unique creative nexuses of the 20th century. Emphasizing
creativity and freedom, BMC nurtured an extraordinary cast of
practitioners of all types from dancers and designers to poets and
painters. BMC’s teachers and students dramatically changed the
worlds of art and education in the US and beyond.
The Black Mountain College Museum + Arts Center
(BMCM+AC), founded in 1993 in Asheville (about 15 miles from
the college’s old site), is dedicated to preserving BMC’s history and
continuing its legacy through an active series of programs and
publications. Every fall BMCM+AC hosts an incredible gathering
called REVIEWING Black Mountain College, an interdisciplinary
conference where researchers and enthusiasts present findings and
new perspectives on the school. One of the most captivating reg-
ular speakers is David Silver, professor and chair of environmental
studies at the University of San Francisco, who has presented at
the conference every year for the past Io years. David’s passion and
charisma shine through when he speaks about BMC’s often over-
looked farming operation, which ran for the length of the school’s
existence and engaged so many of its students, faculty, and staff.
David’s deep research and attention to detail is awe-
inspiring; so is his enthusiasm as he recounts the names and types
of animals, every student involved in the farm's upkeep, and the

el.text: minutiae of what it took to run a farm on the grounds of one of the
world's most famous art colleges. Through robust, dedicated, and
original research, David’s book sheds light on the land’s significance
and impact on college life.
The farm was crucial to BMC’s mission, providing students
with hands-on learning opportunities and promoting sustain-
able agriculture practices—not to mention feeding the college’s
residents. David has not only looked over every timetable and all
accounts kept at the farm, he’s transformed anecdotes and ephem-
era into a cohesive and captivating narrative that tells the story
of the land and the people who made it happen, as it’s never been
told before.
The Farm at Black Mountain College offers fresh perspec-
tives on the creative life of the school by examining how the farm
provided the conditions for significant innovations in craft, perfor-
mance, drawing, photography, painting, sculpture, and writing.
It vividly describes the farm’s inauspicious beginnings, in 1933,
and the fruitful relationships with local organizations that helped
it thrive. The book introduces a new cast of characters to BMC lore
and shows how some of the college’s most recognized names, like
artists Josef Albers and Ruth Asawa, were involved in its upkeep.
Significantly, this compelling narrative challenges the conventional
understanding that BMC was an isolated utopia and provides a
fresh perspective on how the college’s philosophy of experiential
learning and collaboration influenced students’ artistic work,
ultimately shaping much of the American art scene.
We sincerely thank David for his exceptional work bringing
this story to life. Through his creativity, he has produced a cap-
tivating collection of ideas, showcased in this book and the exhi-
bition, The Farm at Black Mountain College College, co-curated by
Bruce Johansen, on view at BMCM+AC from 27 September 2024
to II January 2025.
The Farm at Black Mountain College is a remarkable
project that showcases the work of many artists and collaborators.
It is made possible thanks to major support from the North
Carolina Humanities, an organization devoted to connecting
North Carolinians through culture experiences. We are also
deeply grateful to the Wyeth Foundation for American Art, the
Ruth Foundation for the Arts, and the Windgate Foundation for
their contributions.
Thanks go to Bruce Johansen, co-curator of The Farm
at Black Mountain College, Heather South, Lead Archivist
of the Western Regional Archives, the State Archives of North
Carolina; Abel Weinrib; and the Center for Creative Photography.
We also want to express our deep gratitude to Emma Singleton
for her exceptional design work, which gave life to this book.
Finally we thank the entire BMCM+AC and Atelier Editions
teams who have worked tirelessly to make this book a reality.
The BMCM+AC team includes Alice Sebrell, Kira Houston, Maya
Rosenbaum, Maru McCoy, Holly Filsinger, and the BMCM+AC
Board of Directors. The Atelier Editions editorial team includes
Kingston Trinder and editor Ananda Pellerin, who worked closely
with David to shape this book. David and Ananda’s combined
effort and unwavering dedication have played a crucial
role in bringing these stories to a wide audience for the first time.
David’s work sheds light on BMC’s interdisciplinary
approach and its commitment to social and ecological engage-
ment through transformative practices that extend beyond the
boundaries of the art world. Similarly, this book is the result of
a longstanding collaboration between BMCM+AC and Atelier
Editions, one that echoes the spirit that united some of the most
dedicated believers in the farm at Black Mountain College.

el.text: The bullying began as the five men piled into
art and writing student Tom Field’s Buick
Roadster. It continued for four miles, down and
around the curvy mountain roads from Black
Mountain College to Ma Peak’s, the local tav-
ern. Over multiple rounds of Ballantine Ale the
needling escalated, coming mostly from writing
professor Robert Creeley and art student Dan
Rice, and focused exclusively on Tom. Some of
the taunting was homophobic, some stemmed
from jealousy of Tom’s superior painting skills,
some was fueled by literal hunger. By then—late
summer 1955—the last Black Mountain College
farmer was long gone, and the campus, which
had come to rely on the now-collapsed farm for
subsistence, was in the grips of a severe food
crisis. Fuming, Tom drove his tormentors back
to campus. The bullying did not cease.
At his wits' end, Tom aimed his car at
Meadows Inn, the two-story cottage he shared
with other students, and pushed the pedal to
the metal. A massive Boom/, then silence, then
groans. The Buick had rammed against the
fieldstone chimney and rested, student Michael
Rumaker remembered, “like an accordion.” The
cottage shook, then shuddered, then was still.
“It was a battlefield,” recalled college
rector Charles Olson of the post-crash scene.
“The place was strewn with these bodies—
broken backs, broken hips.” An hour later, after
the injured had been carted off to the hospi-
tal, a confused sheriff surveyed the scene and
scratched his head. He’d seen everything, he
said to no one in particular, but “I have never
heard of a man driving his own car into his
own home.”
More than two decades earlier, in 1933, and
against all odds, Black Mountain College (BMC)
was established in Western North Carolina, just
outside of Asheville. From the start the small,
rural liberal arts college was a radical depar-
ture from other institutions of higher education.
Faculty owned the college. Students, faculty, and
a small staff operated it together. There were no
departmental chairs, deans, provosts, or presi-
dents, and certainly no board of trustees. Fine
arts, music, theater, and dance were placed at
the center of the curriculum. Learning by doing
was encouraged, and students were expected to
take ownership of their education. Most striking,
the college was communal. Students, faculty,
and faculty families lived, studied, worked, and
socialized together.
Funds were always an issue. The school
survived through the Great Depression and
World War II, partially on the kindness of
donors, but also on the rewards reaped by hard-
working members of the BMC community who
kept the campus farm producing food. Despite
these earlier efforts, throughout the 1950s, with
no money and a wayward faculty and student
body, the college started to crumble, ultimately
collapsing in 1956—just a year after the fateful
car crash.
The story that’s already been told time and
again is that despite its perpetual financial woes,
remote location, and brief 23-year existence,

el.text: Black Mountain College attracted a jaw-drop-
ping band of famous and soon-to-be famous art-
ists, writers, thinkers, and visionaries from the
US, Europe, and beyond, a veritable who’s who
of mid-20th-century Western art and ideas. An
abridged list of faculty and students includes
Anni and Josef Albers, Ruth Asawa, John Cage,
Robert Creeley, Merce Cunningham, Willem de
Kooning, Robert Duncan, Buckminster Fuller,
Paul Goodman, Ray Johnson, Franz Kline, Jacob
Lawrence, Robert Motherwell, Charles Olson,
Robert Rauschenberg, M. C. Richards, and Cy
Twombly. Nearly all books and exhibitions
about Black Mountain College focus on the
famous folk who taught, visited, or studied at
the school.
This book is different. The Farm at Black
Mountain College follows renegade students,
faculty, farmers, and community partners as
they start and sustain a campus farm in the
1930s, build a better farm in the 1940s, and
watch it all collapse in the 1950s. What emerges
is a new cast of characters with riveting sto-
ries that shed a brighter light on what exactly
happened at BMC through the decades. The
farm was of vital importance to the college,
not only because it provided necessary food
from organic farming, but because it served
as a testing ground for self-sufficiency, com-
munal living, and collaboration—the most pre-
cious and precarious ingredient at the college.
In these pages, the spotlight is on the extraordi-
nary contributions of these folk, many of whose
stories have seldom, if ever, been explored.
The Farm at Black Mountain College is
the product of extensive archival research.
Over the last decade, I have made a dozen
trips to the Western Regional Archives (WRA)
in Asheville, North Carolina, to immerse
myself in their Black Mountain College
Collection. I have conducted research using
other BMC-related collections at ten other
archives and centers, including the Black
Mountain College Museum + Arts Center,
the Getty Research Institute, the Swannanoa
Valley Museum & History Center, and
University of Arizona’s Center for Creative
Photography. I have also had the privilege
of speaking with ten former Black Mountain
College students—Mary Daniels, Ted
Dreier Jr, Marita Pevsner Dresner, Martha
King, Trueman MacHenry, Ron Robertson,
Dorothea Rockburne, Claude Stoller, Marie
Tavroges Stilkind, and Martha Treichler—
most of whom lit up at the very mention
of the farm.
A NOTE ON NAMES
Whenever possible, I refer to people by the names their peers
used. For example, Mary “Molly” Gregory, faculty of woodworking,
was called Molly, not Professor Gregory or similar. In cases where
I am unsure what they were called, I use the standard practice of
referring to them by their last names.

el.text: Anne “Nan” Howard Chapin, Rollins College student and dropout, and founding member
and student of Black Mountain College, 1934.
Without Nan Chapin, there is no Black Mountain College. Born
in 1913, Anne “Nan” Howard Chapin grew up in Stafford Springs,
Connecticut, the youngest of six children raised on a shoestring
budget by her widowed mother, Anne. When Nan was I5, her
mother married Colonel Arthur S. Dwight, a well-to-do engineer.
The family moved to Dwight’s home in Great Neck, Long Island, the
new-money town that F. Scott Fitzgerald used as a model for arriv-
iste suburb West Egg in The Great Gatsby. With a deep interest in
experimental education, Anne persuaded Nan to attend the School
of Organic Education in Fairhope, Alabama, for two winters during
her junior and senior years of high school. Founded by education
reformer Marietta Johnson, the school espoused progressive prin-
ciples by eliminating tests and grades, offering students active,
group, and experiential learning environments, and encouraging
community building. Through her experiences in Alabama, Nan,
who pulled her hair back into a ponytail and whose conventional
style belied her open-minded nature, started to develop her own
interest in unconventional education. When it came to thinking
about college, she found Rollins College, in the small leafy city of
Winter Park, Florida, near Orlando, most interesting. !
In 1930 Rollins College was indeed interesting. Five years
earlier, Hamilton Holt, former editor and publisher of the liberal
weekly magazine The Independent, master of generating publicity,
and possessor of mildly innovative ideas about education reform,
had become president of the sleepy liberal arts college. Through
tireless fundraising, especially among the wealthy inhabitants of
Winter Park, Holt had raised enough money to rebuild the campus
in a Spanish-Mediterranean style, dominated by white stucco and
orange tile roofs, and secured commissions to build a new library,
theater, dormitory, and the Knowles Memorial Chapel. With a huge
donation from Frances Knowles Warren, made in memory of her
father, one of the college’s original trustees, Holt commissioned
world-renowned college and church architect, Ralph Adams Cram,
to replicate a 17th-century classical chapel Cram had seen in Toledo,
Spain. Holt established new interdisciplinary professorships with
provocative titles like “Professor of Books,” “Professor of Evil,” and
“Professor of Leisure,” which he filled with what he called “golden
personalities” who would, ideally, ignite engagement among stu-
dents. He curbed traditional lectures and classroom recitations,
replacing them with small group discussions and one-on-one
meetings between student and professor. Students were granted
near freedom to pursue electives related to their own interests. 2
For three years, Nan poured her mind and muscle into
Rollins College. She got good grades and was a sorority sister of

el.text: Gamma Phi Beta, where she became best friends with Elizabeth
“Betty” Young and Sara “Sally” Sylvester. Nan was also a mem-
ber of the Glee Club, the Student Association, the International
Relations Club, Le Cercle Frangais, Rollins Literary Society, and
the Cosmopolitan Club. She was especially active in the Rollins
Theatre Workshop, where she worked closely with drama professor
Robert “Bob” Wunsch. Throughout the 1932-33 school year, she
accompanied Wunsch to nearby Eatonville where a young Zora
Neale Hurston was writing, rehearsing, and directing a community
play that would become From Sun to Sun. Visiting night after night
to watch rehearsals, Nan recalled being followed by local Ku Klux
Klan members who would tell her and Wunsch to stay where they
belonged. Nan continued attending the rehearsals, as well as the
actual play, and worked with Wunsch to stage From Sun to Sun at
Rollins. Although Holt agreed to host the play, he demanded it take
place in the Recreation Hall, rather than the college’s new Annie
Russell Theatre, and that the all-Black cast perform to a whites-
only audience. Holt may have considered himself a progressive,
but his decisions were influenced by the status quo.3
While Nan enjoyed theater, her favorite class at Rollins was
whatever class John Andrew Rice was teaching. Like Nan, Rice
had arrived at Rollins in September 1930. He was one of Holt’s hot-
shots, hired to teach classics. Already forced out of three schools
(the Webb School, the University of Nebraska, and the New Jersey
College for Women), Rice arrived with a reputation as a cam-
pus gadfly, burner of bridges, and phenomenal teacher. A Rhodes
Scholar and master of Socratic dialogue, he would enter a class-
room, light his pipe, ask a few questions, and let the conversation
take over. Nan especially enjoyed his Athenian Civilization class in
which students would consider what constituted an “ideal college,”
and how such considerations could and should apply to Rollins.
Rice relentlessly encouraged students to explore not just ideas, but
their own preconceived notions of those ideas. Sometimes the
discussion was so interesting that when the end-of-class bell rang,
students would rise from their chairs, walk out of the classroom,
cross a few well-manicured lawns, circle a lake, and climb the stairs
to the large patio outside Rice’s cottage where they would continue
the discussion over iced tea for several more hours. Many of Rice’s
neighbors, including Theodore “Ted” Dreier, faculty of physics,
and his wife Bobbie, joined the lively conversations. “Rollins was
sort of rocking,” Bobbie recalled. “Rice made a there, there.”4
Despite his loyal student following, Rice was a bully. In
class, he taunted and teased intellectually weaker students, often
bringing them to tears. “He got a kick out of putting people down

when they were stupid,” remembered Bobbie. A shortish, pudgy,
tweed-wearing man who perpetually had a pipe in his mouth, Rice
had a reputation for impropriety in all regards. One day, a potential
donor was touring the campus when she came upon Rice sunbath-
ing in the backyard of his college housing, dressed in “extremely
revealing underwear.” Unfazed, Rice stood up and conversed with
the shocked woman for 15 minutes. As art historian Lewis Shelley

caused him to be condemned by a small segment of people in the
conservative community.” Dreier put it simply: “He antagonized
the donors.”

To make matters worse, Rice chaired or was a member of
multiple faculty committees that assessed several of President
Holt’s most cherished initiatives. In spring 1932, for example,
Rice chaired a faculty committee that recommended abolishing
fraternities and sororities on campus, claiming they favored rich
students and encouraged class divisions and cliques. Holt, as
well as some alumni and donors, understood the report as a per-
sonal attack. Then, in fall 1932, Rice served on a committee exam-
ining Holt’s deep cuts in faculty salaries, a decision the president
argued was caused by the Great Depression. The committee’s
report, written by Rice, reached an entirely different conclusion,
namely that the source of the college’s deficit was Holt’s building
spree. Lastly, Rice helped write a report in favor of eliminating
one of Holt’s curriculum models that was creative but confusing to
students and faculty. Holt was livid.’
Finally, in spring 1933, Holt fired Rice, a tenured professor,
for being “very, very indiscreet, and worse than that, quite intoler-
ant, and worse than that, insulting.” By the end of the semester, rep-
resentatives from the American Association of University Professors
(AAUP) were called to campus to convene a public hearing on the
matter. The hearing took place in Knowles Chapel for a full ten
days and consisted mostly of Holt personally reading 52 letters and
signed statements from students, faculty, staff, and townspeople
against Rice. Some were petty or amusing (one testimony accused
Rice of walking around the college’s beach house in a jockstrap, to
which the classics professor retorted, “I’ve never worn a jockstrap
in my life!”), while others contained accusations of bullying. A few
days after the public hearing and that year’s graduation, Holt fired
five more professors, including Frederick Georgia (chemistry) and
Ralph Lounsbury (political science), accusing them of supporting
Rice. Holt wanted to fire physics professor Dreier but hesitated,
since he was the nephew of Margaret Dreier Robins, a wealthy and
influential trustee. Out of protest, Dreier, and later Wunsch, resigned.
By mid-June, the purge was complete: nine out of 45 Rollins profes-
sors had been fired, forced to resign, or had resigned out of protest.
Nan was furious and quickly rallied fellow students into
action. Together with Nathaniel “Nat” French, Rollins’ student
body president, and George Barber, editor of the student newspaper
The Sandspur, Nan led a student delegation that met with Holt to
proclaim their unwavering support for Professor Rice. When that
didn’t work, Nan and others organized a campus protest. When
that didn’t work, Nat and Barber invited the local press to campus
and announced they were leaving the college. When that didn’t
work, Nan organized the final action: she and over a dozen Rollins
students dropped out. Dejected, Nan returned to her family home
in Great Neck. It was early June 1933.9

Later that evening, the Colonel invited his friend William S.
Barstow to stop by. An electrical engineer who had made a small
fortune in public utility investment banking, Barstow listened to
Rice’s pitch, witnessed Dwight’s exuberance, and declared, “If the
Colonel’s going to put up a thousand dollars, I will, too!” Amidst
all the excitement, Nan boldly declared that she would be attend-
ing the new college, making her its first student. As the night came
to an end in Great Neck, Rice departed with $2,000 in seed money,
one full-paying student, and a summer home for his family.
STARTING A COLLEGE
The very next day Nan hit the ground running by taking charge of
student recruitment. First, she contacted a number of Rollins rebels,
shared the idea for a new college, and asked if they could commit
to $1,000 a year for tuition and board. Her friends from the Student
Association, Nat French and George Barber, were early enthusiasts,
as was Betty, Nan’s former sorority sister, who was shocked when
her conservative parents approved.
Next, Nan assigned geographic regions to the early commits
so they could recruit prospective students. While former Rollins
student and water polo player Ed Jenks canvased Philadelphia,
Nat, boyishly handsome and on crutches due to polio, covered the
Boston and Cambridge areas. Nan took the tristate area of New
York, New Jersey, and Connecticut, meeting with fellow Glee Club
member Mary Trowbridge, International Relations Club member
Everett “Ev” Dwight, and former Rollins schoolmate Norm Weston.
Together Nan, Nat, and Jenks kept in touch with Rice and others. "!
Nan’s smartest move was to organize a gathering of commit-
ted students in New York City where they wrote a collective letter
announcing the new college and sent it to other Rollins students,
current and former, inviting them to join. The letter read:
We, the undersigned students, who have participated
in the organization of Black Mountain College, join
with the members of the faculty in presenting for
your consideration the enclosed announcement of
the college.
We feel that you would appreciate the opportunity to
participate with a congenial group in a thoroughly
cooperative educational enterprise. We are confident
that the things that were talked about at Rollins can

It must have felt empowering for these young people, especially
during a time of grave financial uncertainty, to take control of their
educational pathways. It must have felt exciting, during an era in
which everything seemed to be on pause, to strive toward some-
thing with conviction. Whatever the case, as a result of their spir-
ited letter, five would-be seniors at Rollins—Sydney Carter, Laura
Belle Fisher, Marcella Martin, Alice Lee Swan, and Sally Sylvester—
left Rollins and agreed to come on board. As August came to an
end, the college had more than 15 committed students. !2
With Nan leading the recruitment charge, Dreier and Rice
focused their efforts on fundraising. From the beginning, Dreier—
blond, boyish, and with seemingly unending reserves of physical
energy and idealism—was the money guy. Maybe this was because
he came from a lot of money. Born in 1902 in Brooklyn Heights to
a family that had inherited a fortune made in the iron trade, Dreier’s
extended family, especially the women, were active leaders in social
reform and the arts. His mother, Ethel Eyre Dreier, was president
of the Women’s City Club of New York and head of the Women’s
Suffrage Party of Brooklyn. His aunt, Margaret Dreier Robins, was
president of the National Women’s Trade Union League and, among
other things, had been a trustee at Rollins College but resigned
in protest when Rice got fired. Another of Ted’s aunts, Katherine
Dreier, was a painter who, along with Marcel Duchamp and Man
Ray, founded the Société Anonyme, an organization that promoted
modern and avant-garde art. '3
In 1921 while still enrolled at Harvard, first to study geol-
ogy and later electrical engineering, Dreier became best friends
with his roommate Malcolm “Mac” Forbes. When he graduated,
Dreier married Barbara “Bobbie” Loines, who came from an equally
wealthy and social reform-minded family. After working five years
as an engineer at General Electric, the course of Dreier’s life would
change in late summer 1930 when the head of Rollins’ physics
department was killed in a car accident. With a recommendation
from Forbes, who by then was teaching psychology at Rollins, Holt
interviewed and hired Dreier as an assistant professor of physics.
For three years Dreier did nothing to distinguish himself at Rollins,
except near the end when he resigned to protest the firing of Rice. '4
Dreier began his fundraising efforts for the new college
close to home. His parents, Henry Edward and Ethel, got things
started with a $2,000 contribution. Next, Dreier hit the road to tap
into his and wife Bobbie’s extensive family networks. Oftentimes
the pair would bring along Nan, who charmed potential donors
with her bright insights into what progressive education could and
should be. With her help the Dreiers secured a modest $500 from
family friends. '5
Though he had a rocky start of it, Rice would eventually
prove a more successful fundraiser. He managed to secure meet-
ings with higher-ups at both the Carnegie Foundation and the
Rockefeller Foundation, but each time he was asked for something

In early October 1933, Helen Boyden, a Radcliffe-trained
economics instructor at the two-week-old Black Mountain College,
received a book in the mail from a friend. It was Ralph Borsodi’s
Flight from the City: An Experiment in Creative Living on the Land,
published earlier that year. The book followed the author, his wife
Myrtle Mae, and their two young sons’ flight from Manhattan,
where Borsodi worked in advertising, to rural Upstate New York
where they started a homestead, a modest dwelling combining
subsistence agriculture with do-it-yourself food preservation,
and driven by the goal of self-sufficiency. The Borsodis grew and
canned their own food, raised livestock, and made, sewed, and
built as much as they could. Along the way Borsodi kept detailed
financial logs of costs and savings, and discovered that with help
from modern technologies, such as tillers in the garden and an
electric mixer in the kitchen, the homestead was able to turn a mod-
est profit. “It was a romantic vision,” Boyden recalled over three
decades later about one of the effects the Great Depression had
on family life. “Since there were no jobs in the city, there was quite
a movement back to the countryside.” Boyden passed the book
along to one of her new students, John Applegate, not knowing
that within a week or so the book would pass through dozens of
student hands. Borsodi’s withdrawal from urban life and quest for
self-sufficiency on a rural, modern homestead resonated with these
optimistic students and faculty looking for a new way to live and
learn. By the end of October, Boyden remembered, Flight from the
City “swept the college like wildfire.” '9

his last. In late spring 1932, Solebury hosted Holt, who told of how
Rollins had done away with traditional lectures and classroom rec-

that Rollins did not require College Board Exams, SAT-like tests
that Weston had bombed earlier that spring. That was the clincher.
After graduation he returned home and somehow managed to con-

THE FARM DEBATE
A new college requires ample discussions and decisions. For
that, Black Mountain College established three administrative
bodies, all comprised of students and faculty, with no full-time
administrators, as per Rice’s wishes. The Student Committee
addressed student-related issues, the Faculty Committee decided
on curricular issues, and the Board of Fellows was responsible
for the college’s finances and the hiring and firing of faculty. When
larger issues arose, students, faculty, faculty families, and staff—
the whole BMC community—were invited to participate in general
meetings. Decisions were reached painstakingly through consen-
sus. In early December of that year, six students were granted a
general meeting to discuss whether or not the college should start
a campus farm. This meeting would set the tone for many meetings
to come, it was long, democratic, and full of drama.
It began with fire.3! All afternoon a work crew of students
and faculty had chopped dead chestnut trees into logs for a huge
evening blaze in the fireplace in Lee Hall’s cavernous lobby. Chairs

NORM’S FARM SEMINAR
Throughout that first year Norm spent most of his time learning
double-entry bookkeeping from Dreier and quickly became the
college’s assistant bookkeeper. “As time went,” Norm recalled,
“I became less and less of a student and more of a bookkeeper.” The
only class that engaged him was Farm Seminar. The independent
study’s goal was ambitious: learn from local farmers and produce
a detailed, affordable, and immediately executable five-year farm
plan for Black Mountain College. Norm plunged in.
Starting in November and lasting through spring, Norm
would jump into his Buick and drive about eight miles from Blue
Ridge to Swannanoa to visit the Asheville Farm School. Established
in 1894 by the women of the Presbyterian Church, the Asheville
Farm School provided education for poor, rural boys. Because most
of the boys had no prior schooling, much of the school’s curricu-
lum was vocational. And because few of the boys could afford to pay
tuition, they worked for it, primarily on the school’s farm. In 1933,
the Asheville Farm School was run by Dr Henry S. Randolph, a
charismatic educator trained in progressive education. Supervising
the farm was Bernhard Laursen, who grew up in Denmark, studied
agriculture in Germany, and taught farming, gymnastics, and folk
dancing. Most times Norm would barrage the patient Laursen with
questions about farming. Laursen also visited the BMC farm-to-be,
offering all kinds of useful suggestions about soil quality, planting,
and livestock. 36
Norm made regular visits to the Swannanoa Test Farm as
well. Located about ten miles from campus in Oteen, it was one of
six such test farms in the state, all run through the North Carolina
Department of Agriculture, offering free, professional agricultural
advice to locals in order to stimulate the local economy and encour-
age agricultural productivity. Often joined by Bailey (who pumped
"poultry man" Jones with questions about chickens) and Nat (who
studied the farm’s buildings and structures), Norm would meet
with S. C. Clapp to learn more about day-to-day farming operations.
Clapp was an active researcher in soil management, and his lessons
focused primarily on building healthy soil with techniques we would
now call organic gardening, including crop rotation, companion
planting, and cover crops. Clapp encouraged Norm to build up the

chopped wood for fires and hauled coal for the furnaces. Early on,
weekday afternoons were left unscheduled, so that members of the
BMC community could exercise. This meant visiting the gymna-
sium to play basketball, badminton, and handball, swimming in
the pool (a concrete basin filled by a brook), or taking a hike in the
surrounding mountains.
By year two, things began to change. While weekday after-
noons remained unscheduled, more and more students, faculty,

to me and a very pleasant one,” he wrote. 46

THE BUILDER
Nathaniel “Nat” Stowers French was born in 1912 in Boston, the
first of three children of Eleanor Campbell Fisher and John R. P.
French, headmaster of Derby Academy, in Hingham, Massachusetts,
and later headmaster at the prestigious and progressive Cambridge
Academy, in Weston, Mass. Young Nat was busy. Active in Boy
Scouts for years, he achieved the highest rank of Eagle Scout. An
athlete, Nat played football and hockey; he swam, sailed, and canoed.
In high school he was a leader: president of his class, chairman
of student council, and captain of the football team. Academically,
he struggled but survived. To make money, he chopped and
sold wood. 48
In 1930, Nat followed his father’s footsteps to Harvard, with
a desire to become a headmaster himself. Socially, he excelled.
He enjoyed intramural football and hockey and served as manager
of the swim team. According to Evarts, Nat was “husky, athletic,
one of the boys, fond of dancing—and ready for almost any excite-
ment.” His performance in the classroom was another matter.
Academically he struggled mightily and by the middle of his first
year at Harvard, he was placed on probation. By the end of his first
year, he had failed out. With an aggressive intervention from his
father, Harvard reinstated Nat after he passed a summer class. 49
On his first day as a Harvard sophomore, Nat left Cambridge
to cross the Charles River and by the time he reached Boston, he
had lost all use of his legs. He “laid flat on his back with infantile
paralysis,” as he recalled. He returned home to recover from what

For the most part, members of Black Mountain College adored the
Blue Ridge campus. They loved the way everyone came together
in Lee Hall, in pairs and small groups, as classes and committees,
and as a campus community. They enjoyed the natural surround-
ings, the pathways between the buildings, the hikes up and down
the surrounding mountains, and the view of the Blue Ridge range.
They even learned to tolerate packing up their belongings each
summer and scattering away. The problem was their landlord.
Dr Willis Duke Weatherford, born and raised in Black
Mountain, was, among many other things, president of the Blue
Ridge Assembly and the Blue Ridge campus’s landlord. Although
the relationship between Black Mountain College and Weatherford
began cordially, it soon soured. When the college inquired about
purchasing Blue Ridge, Weatherford was dismissive. Most frustrat-
ing was that each year, the college tried to negotiate a long-term
lease and each year Weatherford refused. Some years, students and
faculty would leave the college at the end of spring term uncer-
tain whether Blue Ridge would be theirs in the fall. In June 1936,
the college managed to extract a five-year lease, the longest in its
three-year history. But there was a catch. The agreement stipulated
that Weatherford could lease or sell Blue Ridge to anyone willing
to pay a higher sum. Tired of the uncertainty and distrustful of
Weatherford, the college looked to greener pastures and purchased
Lake Eden in May 1937.68
Located five miles from Blue Ridge, Lake Eden was devel-
oped in 1923 by E. W. Grove as a camp for girls. When that venture
didn’t work out, it was run as a summer resort. Lake Eden’s 667
acres were graced with a human-made lake, woods, pastures, and
farmable land. Scattered about the property were 14 buildings,
including two large lodges suitable for student dormitories, a lake-
side dining room, a handful of small, two-story cottages suitable
for faculty lodgings, a farmhouse, and a bathhouse. To meet the
steep purchase price of $35,000 (a $2,000 down payment and
$7,000 a year for five years), the college sent a panicked appeal to
BMC alumni and supporters. A gift of $12,500 from former student
Stephen Forbes and nearly $1,000 from Dreier’s parents allowed
the college to purchase Lake Eden in May 1937.
Besides gaining more space, the college community also
gained more time—namely, summers. While they’d grown accus-
tomed to vacating Blue Ridge each May, Lake Eden was theirs and
they thought they could stay all year. This led, beginning in sum-
mer 1944 and lasting through summer 1953, to a series of Summer
Institutes, usually organized around art and music. They generally
ran for one or two months, were organized around a set of classes,

tete: The Farm at Black Mountain College

el.text: and gave attendees—BMC and visiting students and faculty—time
and space to dig deeply into a topic without having to participate
in the college’s everyday tasks and tensions. These seasonal ses-
sions attracted some of the famous artists and thinkers that are
now synonymous with the college, including John Cage, Merce
Cunningham, Buckminster Fuller, and Jacob Lawrence. They
were also responsible for some extraordinary artistic develop-
ments, including Cage’s “Theater Piece No. I,” widely recognized
as the first “happening”; the formation of the pioneering Merce
Cunningham Dance Company; and Fuller’s first attempt (unsuc-
cessful) to erect a large-scale geodesic dome. Less ambitious,
but no less important, the college was also able to offer regular
classes during summer, usually referred to as summer sessions,
allowing existing students to continue their studies while giving
new and prospective students an opportunity to test out the
innovative college.
Full of potential, Lake Eden had two major problems. First,
it had no heating and therefore was uninhabitable in winter (throw-
ing into question the dream of a year-round residency). Second,
it had neither classrooms nor studios for students to paint, write,
or study. Lake Eden needed work, work required money, and the
college had little if any of that. It would take more than four years
before the college finally moved to Lake Eden, during which time
they stayed at Blue Ridge thanks to that final, longer lease.
While the move took some time, the college still had a pres-
ence at the new location. Almost immediately after the purchase
was finalized, Dreier, Norm, and Bas began making regular trips
to assess current and potential farming operations at Lake Eden.
Enlisting once again the good advice of Laursen and Clapp, they
were able to assess the soil (poor) and estimate how much labor
was required (a lot) to bring the land to working condition. “There
was hardly anything here that could be called a farm at all,” wrote
woodworking professor Molly Gregory years later. Nevertheless,
the college was optimistic and the solution was clear. A few times
a week, a work crew piled into the college truck and drove five miles
to Lake Eden to clear fields and plant row after row of cover crops
to improve the soil. During the 1937-38 school year they managed
to plant over ten acres of crimson clover. The next year, they planted
nearly 15 acres of crimson clover, 12 acres of soybeans, and seven
acres of rye. They also hauled Nat’s pigpen and pigs to the new
campus and built a small, modest barn. 7°
The most dramatic farm-related development, however,
was the addition of the college’s first farmer, Roscoe “Ross” Penley.
A local Black Mountain inhabitant, Penley, a “ruddy, boxy man
exuding strength,” joined Black Mountain College in January 1938.
Although he lacked managerial skills, Penley had more than enough
farming skills (and family help) to maintain the Blue Ridge farm
while simultaneously preparing the burgeoning farm at Lake Eden.
More importantly, Penley was both good-natured and infinitely
patient. “We'd ask him all sorts of questions,” student Ike Nakata
recalled. “What kind of tree is that? What’s the name of that wild
flower? Is that wild plant good to eat? How do you sharpen a hoe?
How do you use a scythe? Did he like the Navy? Did he ever get
drunk? Did he think he’d ever amount to anything?”7!
Perhaps best of all for the financially struggling college was
the agreement leasing Blue Ridge farm, farmhouse, and farm tools
to the Penley family: Ross, wife Stella, and their three sons Max,
Jack, and Atlas. In return Ross promised the college one-third of all
harvests, including grapes and apples. Further, he agreed to take
care of the hogs and horse, with the college supplying feed. At Lake
Eden Penley helped clear fields, plant cover crops, and would, in the

In late spring as Norm raced around making final adjust-
ments for Lake Eden Inn, something momentous occurred: the
arrival of William Morse Cole and his wife Fanny. To reassure its
initial supporters, the college had secured the services of Cole, a
professor of accounting at the Harvard Business School, to prepare
the college’s annual budget. In return, the Coles would take ten
days of vacation on campus and Cole would give a lecture or two
on Shakespeare. Cole and Norm got along famously. After audit-
ing books together for four years, the elder of the two exclaimed,
“Norm, you are wasting your time here. You ought to go to the
Harvard Business School.” In response, Norm pointed out that
he did not have a college degree and, come to think of it, wasn’t
even close to getting one from Black Mountain College. Cole
dismissed the lack of degree as a technicality. ’5
As well as employment and summer housing, the inn brought
in $875 (equivalent to about $18,000 in 2024) for the college that
year and also managed some community outreach. Throughout the
summer 65 boys and girls and one Reverend J. H. Gruver from
the Mountain Orphanage swam in Lake Eden in exchange for pay-
ing 25 cents per hour to a BMC student-lifeguard, a tradition that
would continue for the next five summers. This is all to say that the
venture was a huge success, laying the groundwork for prosper-
ous Lake Eden Inn summers to come. Despite this achievement,
after more than five years at Black Mountain College, Norm was
ready for something new—and so was Nan. Although the college
never obtained accreditation (primarily due to not meeting state
and national standards on faculty salaries, endowment, number of
books in the library, and ample science equipment), it did, on rare
occasion, grant degrees to students, which were sometimes recog-
nized by prestigious schools like Harvard and Yale. In 1936, Nan
graduated with a degree in history and worked for two years with
Wunsch in the drama department. The August 1938 birth of her
and Norm’s son Michael led the couple to reassess their priorities.
“We cannot stay in this utopian situation forever,” Nan recalled
saying to Norm. “We’d better get a little more practical.” 76
In some ways, it was the season for exits. Although John
Andrew Rice had a few good years at Black Mountain College, his
old ways soon re-appeared. For his frequent tangles with faculty and
students and his consistent embroilment in this or that college con-
troversy, Rice, by fall 1937, had strained relationships with Albers,
Dreier, and Wunsch and frequent—and public—rows with wife, Nell.
He did not share the students’ love for farming nor Dreier’s spiri-
tual bliss over labor, and he preferred old, staid Lee Hall over the
modernist models he saw for Lake Eden. Worse, Rice fancied, flirted

which had run more than a half dozen stories about the innovative

Rice, and Colonel Dwight, BMC’s original funder, refused future

climbed into the trusty Buick and drove to visit him. Although

eventually resigned in February 1940. His book, I Came Out of
the Eighteenth Century, was published in 1942 and won the pres-

his conversation with Professor Morse fresh on his mind, Norm
came to a decision. In December 1938, the Weston family packed
themselves and their belongings into the faithful Buick and drove
to Cambridge, Massachusetts, launching Norm on his path to a
graduate degree at Harvard Business School. Black Mountain
College said goodbye to two of its founding members, significant
leaders who had helped establish not only the physical campus
with its buildings and plowed land, but the hopeful spirit of BMC
itself. Looking back nearly 60 years later, Norm wrote of his time
at the school, “I suspect that there is no one on whom BMC hada

LEAVING BLUE RIDGE
Not long after the Westons departed, the unscrupulous landlord
Weatherford returned claiming he had landed a ten-year con-
tract with an unnamed local entity. If true, this would mean Black
Mountain College would have to vacate Blue Ridge by September
1940. Even though Weatherford was cagey, the college pan-
icked. Soon after, Weatherford withdrew the ultimatum. However
any sense of relief was short-lived. In January 1939 the landlord
returned to say he had received another offer for a ten-year contract,
this one at terms that far exceeded Black Mountain College’s mea-
sly budget. Dreier and others believed Weatherford was bluffing.
But what if he wasn’t? 79
Fearing they might be without a home, the college commis-
sioned Walter Gropius, founder of the Bauhaus, chair of architecture
at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design, and friend of the college,
along with Marcel Breuer, another Bauhaus refugee, to draw up
plans for a building complex that could house the college’s main
activities and provide living quarters at Lake Eden. The Gropius-
Breuer plan was stunning, modern, and very expensive. Dreier esti-
mated the cost at $500,000 (about $9 million today). To amass
that large sum, an ambitious fundraising campaign was launched
in early January 1940 at New York’s Museum of Modern Art.
A model of the Gropius-Breuer plan was showcased, and Albers
and Gropius gave talks about the college. A second fundraising
campaign followed, but few funds were raised. Monied folk, it
seemed, were reluctant to invest in a college that was still unac-
credited and lacked a board of trustees. Further, within months,
President Franklin D. Roosevelt would request from Congress over
$1 billion in war funds. The US economy was rapidly becoming
a war economy. 80

THE WORK PROGRAM
The building of the barn concretized the rhythm of manual labor at
BMC. While there had been no formal program to facilitate daily
chores at Blue Ridge—chopping wood, hauling coal, and tending to
pigs were all voluntary—this would change at Lake Eden. Overnight,
the newly focused Work Program altered the very time and space
of everyday life at Black Mountain College. Morning classes were
scheduled earlier and afternoon/evening classes scheduled later,
freeing up five-to-six hour chunks of the day for work. Each week-
day and most Saturdays, the BMC community would gather on the
porch of Lee Hall, pile into the back of the college truck, and travel
to Lake Eden for an afternoon of physical labor. Campus, in other
words, became distributed: Students and faculty would discuss ideas
and make art at Blue Ridge, learn skills and build structures at Lake
Eden, and hopefully fit in some social time while squished together
in the back of the truck traveling back and forth between sites. 9!

As the amount of work needed at Lake Eden became abundantly

Friends Service Committee (AFSC), a Quaker organization, and
their two decades’ experience running work camps. An early exam-

that, service learning, the work camps invited college and univer-
sity students to live, work, and participate in areas of economic
turmoil—such as the Mississippi cotton delta or the Pennsylvania
coalfields—for eight weeks in summer. To learn more, Bobbie Dreier
tapped into her family’s social reform network to bring AFSC mem-
ber J. Olcutt Sanders to campus for guidance. The school’s first sum-
mer work camp was initiated in 1940. It enrolled about 20 female
and male students who worked for five hours a day, six days a week,
for which they were paid $65 plus room and board for eight weeks.
Although successful in terms of launching the Lake Eden build
program, the summer 1940 work camp, helmed by Gothe, was run
haphazardly and often overlapped awkwardly with Lake Eden Inn’s
activities. Further, unlike the Friends’ work camps, there was very
little integration between the camp and the community. Some work
campers said the only thing they remember doing was working. !0°
Fortunately the 1941 summer work camp was a vast depar-

held high hopes, was gone. Although he had successfully estab-

forward, Gothe was hated by the students. He barked out instruc-

and got enraged when they didn’t. “He ran the organization like

prompting a collective sigh of relief. 1°!

By mid-May 1942 the barn was complete. At 54 ft long,

Everyone dressed up and the dancing lasted for hours, with live

By all accounts Bill Hanchett was a reliable, hardworking young
man. Born into an affluent family in Evanston, Illinois, in 1922,
William “Bill” Francis Hanchett Jr struggled academically, but
shined as class president. When the Depression wiped out his fam-
ily’s savings, Bill worked in the school cafeteria during lunch, on
a farm after school, and in a factory on weekends to earn money.
In summer 1940, during his sister Alice-Anne’s wedding to Robert
“Bob” Babcock, Hanchett and Babcock got to talking about col-
lege. Hanchett confessed he had neither the grades nor the funds
to attend school. Babcock, who taught political science at Black
Mountain College, regaled him with stories about students and
faculty working together on the farm and constructing campus
buildings. He then hooked his new brother-in-law by noting the
college’s lack of emphasis on grades and its negotiable tuition.
A year later, Bill came to BMC, 105
After a few months on the farm Hanchett found his calling:
raising chickens. Having impressed Penley with his farming skills
and Dreier with his reliability, Hanchett was granted permission
to expand the chicken flock that had been started almost a decade
earlier. “Congratulations are in order!” he wrote to his parents in
mid-March 1942, after a trip to a stock auction in Asheville to pur-
chase Rhode Island Red chicks. “Your farmer correspondent is the
proud guardian of 85 day-old chicks!” To house the chicks, Bill built
a large heated brooder, which would find a home in the basement
of the two-story wooden South Lodge, one of two student dormi-
tories. When only one of his chicks died during the first ten days,
Hanchett’s confidence grew, and he returned to Asheville to pick
up 100 more. Two weeks later he purchased another 100, and by
mid-April Bill was tending over 250 chicks. Albers was so impressed
by his husbandry that he bought eight ducks and gifted them to
Hanchett to raise. 106
And then, just like that, it ended. In late spring 1942, Han-
chett, like so many other young men at the college and across the
country, was drafted. He would be stationed at the US Army Air
Force Base in Douglas, Georgia. Within a year all young, American-
born male BMC faculty were drafted or enlisted into the war effort.
The draft had a dramatic impact on the college’s current male
students too. The 1942-43 school year was like an exodus, recalled
music student Patsy Lynch. “All of the boys left one by one, you
know. Every two weeks or so there’d be a going away party until fin-
ally they all left.” By October 1943, a single male student, Sam Brown,
who suffered from polio, remained at Black Mountain College. 107
Historically, not much attention has been given to the
goings-on at Black Mountain College during the war years. But

tete: The Farm at Black Mountain College

el.text: during this time BMC experienced a flurry of activity performed by
the women who remained on campus. Under the leadership of the
extraordinary Mary “Molly” Gregory, the college spent much of
the war growing all of its food and, against all wartime odds, build-
ing an ambitious series of farm structures. Along the way Molly
assembled a group of female students who would bring the col-
lege closer to self-sufficiency than it ever had been or ever would
be. And when the building process was finished, Black Mountain
College had established a massive capital investment that would
save the college a decade later.
GETTING TO BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE
In 1919 when World War I was over and Molly Gregory was five,
her family moved from Long Island, New York, to Framingham,
Massachusetts, to buy back the family farm. Growing up, Molly, a
scruffy kid with boundless energy, “literally followed the heels of the
farmer,” and became obsessed with growing food, raising animals,
and building farm structures. From age 13 to 18, she attended Beaver
Country Day School, a progressive institution that integrated farm-
ing and woodworking into the curriculum. Molly excelled at art and
developed into a smart, creative, and well-liked student. Even asa
young person, her strong sense of character shone through. Beatrice
W. Van Ness, head of the school’s art department said her “personal-
ity is vigorous and stimulating, and her work reflects the high qual-
ity of her thinking. She has a saving sense of humor and is capable
of carrying much responsibility.” 18
In 1932, Molly entered Vermont’s Bennington College, then
a women’s college, just as it was established. Like Black Mountain
College, Bennington placed visual and performing arts at the cen-
ter of its curriculum. Unlike BMC, the Vermont school planned its
existence for nearly a decade before opening its doors to students.
At Bennington Molly took a wide variety of impressive classes,
including dance with the illustrious Martha Graham and a semes-
ter abroad at the Bermuda Biological Station for Research during
her sophomore year. Her focus, however, was studying sculpture
with Simon Moselsio, a sculptor, painter, and draftsman. Molly’s
roommate and best friend at Bennington was Ruth Bailey, an art
major and younger sister of original BMC student and initiator
of the chicken flock, Dave Bailey. In 1936, Molly became a member
of Bennington's first graduating class. 109
Upon graduating, Molly, short-haired, attractive, always
in flannel tops and blue jeans, and usually holding a cigarette,
established what she called her five-year plan. The idea was simple:
She would find an appealing job, work there for five years, quit,
find another one, and repeat for the rest of her working life. Her
first five-year plan was as a teacher at the prestigious Cambridge
School, in Kendal Green, Massachusetts, led by headmaster John
French, father of Nat. While hired to teach sculpture, Molly also
taught ceramics, painting, and life drawing, and oversaw athletics
and directed the woodshop. She particularly enjoyed her time
with shop teacher Alfred Hulst, who helped Molly refine the
woodworking and building skills she had learned on the family farm.
During her third year at the Cambridge School Molly was
reunited with Ruth Bailey, who arrived to teach art following a
one-year apprenticeship at Black Mountain College. Ruth talked
nonstop about BMC, especially about Josef Albers. When Ruth
visited the campus in spring 1940, Molly tagged along. During her
visit Molly attended classes, led a work day on the farm, and made
an impression on both students and faculty. 110
Dreier in particular was taken by Molly’s enthusiastic
know-how, and over the next year he sent her long letters describ-
ing recent progress on the farm. In spring 1941, Molly and Ruth
visited the college again, but this visit was more like an interview
for Molly. She met with students (who adored her), faculty (who
were impressed by her), and staff (all fans). She also sat in on classes,
attended a general meeting, and visited the modest but full-of-po-
tential farm. Clearly the college wanted Molly, and Molly wanted
the college. But in what capacity? Eventually she was invited to
become a teaching apprentice for Josef Albers, with her modest pay
supported by Ethel Forbes, who, along with husband Mac, was one
of the college’s original funders. Molly was scheduled to start in her
role in fall 1941. She was so excited she arrived that summer. "'1
MOLLY GREGORY AND THE WOODSHOP
Like so many others at Black Mountain College, Molly found Albers’
classes to be exhilarating. “He asked us to look and look,” Molly
recalled, “but, in looking, to trust and to use our own perceptions
creatively and neatly.” Not being a novice, however, she ultimately
felt inhibited in Albers’ classroom and experienced creative blocks.
The solution for this industrious young woman, it seemed, was to
take fewer classes with Albers and teach more of her own. By spring
semester of her first year at BMC, Molly was teaching popular
classes in sculpture and woodworking. '!2
From the start, Black Mountain College had provided
modest opportunities in woodworking, but Molly completely
transformed these opportunities. Shocked at the lack of tools

available her own extensive collection (“a rather shocking amount

The shop produced tables for the dining room, cupboards
for the kitchen, bookshelves for the library, drafting tables for archi-
tecture classes, stools and carving benches for the art room, shelves
for the music room, paper storage racks for the bookbinding shop,
benches for the lobbies inside both the North and South Lodges,
and much more. In November 1942, just over a year after Molly’s
arrival, the woodshop was humming with do-it-yourself activity.
Barbara Heller, a student from New York, was constructing five
benches for the weaving department. Claude Stoller, an architec-
ture student from the Bronx, was busy making a milk rack for the
kitchen. Lou Bernard Voight, professor of landscape architecture
and botany, was constructing cabinets and a table for his study.
And art student Ati Gropius was preparing for a room party by
“making impromptu table settings: grapefruit plates, shallow circles
cut on the lathe into six-inch mahogany squares, a set of delicate
three-pronged forks, and little butter knives from the wood of an
old walnut tree—lathe-shaped, sanded, and oiled.” Countless other
students built rudimentary furniture—chairs, desks, bookshelves,
easels—for their rooms. ''4
With Molly at the helm, the woodshop trained a new genera-
tion of students how to hammer, saw, and drill—how to make things.
Molly also shared her extensive leather skills, gained during her
Bennington days, teaching students how to make their own sandals,
among other things. Within a year, Molly and the woodshop sus-
tained a campus-wide culture of making, a collective behavior that
would help the college through the lean war years and beyond. “It
was asked from the start,” Molly recalled, “that everyone who joined
the community be a contributor, not a purchaser.” ''5
VICTORY FARM
Though much of the land had been cleared and the new barn was
impressive, ambitions to actually develop the farmland at Lake
Eden were coming along slower than expected. The only other
structures were a hastily built small barn and a derelict, unheated
farmhouse, and the only field under cultivation was a single plot
near the farmhouse, which grew more weeds than veggies. Only
one of the pastures was usable because, until then, the main focus
had been soil health. For the last four years Penley had planted and
plowed under acres of cover crops, hoping to reclaim the fields
and pastures, with only a small amount of edible crops planted.
But without Norm to lead, scheduling across the multiple farms fell
largely to Dreier who couldn’t keep up. When it came to delegating
the farm work to other people, Dreier proved equally ineffectual.
BE

He had a reputation for exhorting students to work for some kind
of spiritual enlightenment, micromanaging them when they did
show up, and publicly shaming them when they didn’t. Too often
the plots were planted and tended in fits and bursts and sometimes
yielded more consternation than food. ''6
Although the college would have preferred a slow and steady
buildup of healthy soil and farmland, the country’s involvement
in the war dramatically sped up the process. Led by Dreier, mem-
bers of the college began to make contingency plans for inevita-
ble shortages. A shortage of meat meant raising their own, which
would be difficult since there was also a growing shortage of avail-
able livestock. Further, growing more food and raising more ani-
mals required the construction of structures for storage and shelter,
a daunting task due to shortages of building materials and male
labor, not to mention the college’s perennial cash flow issues. Like
the rest of the country, BMC was facing difficult times.
To Dreier, the solution was clear. Black Mountain College
could and must boost self-sufficiency by growing more food, raising
more animals, and building more farm structures—as quickly and
inexpensively as possible. A farm, he would announce to anyone
within earshot, could profoundly help the college during wartime
by supplying the college with dairy, meat, and vegetables and, like
the victory gardens sprouting up across the country that bolstered
morale while supplying produce, the farm would be a patriotic
contribution to the war effort. Beyond survival and patriotism,
the farm could become a strategic capital investment, a rainy day
fund if difficult times got worse. This was particularly important
since the college had neither a well-developed alumni-donor class
nor a wealthy board of trustees to whom they could turn during
rough stretches. '17
Although Dreier loved dreaming about the farm, building it
was overwhelming. Enter Molly Gregory, who immersed herself in
the farm plan and enjoyed figuring out multi-year planting sched-
ules. She relished balancing forests, fields, and pastures, and cele-
brated when things worked, like when the dairy herd spent a day
grazing the new barley pasture and each cow responded by pro-
ducing two more pounds of milk than usual. Molly also gave Penley
the support he needed. Unlike Dreier, who had assigned the farmer
endless tasks that all seemed to need immediate attention, Molly,
an experienced farmer, was able to think holistically and plan and
prioritize, gaining Penley’s trust and respect. Within a year of living
at Black Mountain College, Molly was managing the farm, and
within a year under her leadership, the farm was humming, pro-
ducing beans, beets, cabbage, carrots, chard, collards, cucumbers,
onions, peas, potatoes, radishes, squash, and tomatoes—amounting
to most of the produce the community ate. ''8
In fact, the farm produced so much food that Black Mountain
College had a surplus. So once a week, Molly gathered up sacks
of vegetables, hopped into the college truck, and drove to Swan-
nanoa and the Asheville Farm School to use their canning machin-
ery. During two weeks in July 1943, Molly and students canned
100 gallons of beets and 85 gallons of beans and put 50 gallons of
kraut into crocks, increasing the college’s winter stores. Though the
operation strengthened the ties between Black Mountain College
and the Asheville Farm School, there was one notable exception.
After Molly was caught smoking in the cannery, in violation of
the school’s smoking ban, the school’s superintendent Henry S.
Randolph angrily called her into his office, had her take a seat, and
glared at her from behind his desk. Molly apologized profusely,
placed a can of beets on his desk, and slowly moved it in his direc-
tion. Randolph accepted both her apology and the beets. ''9
At Lake Eden, acres of field corn, soybean hay, vetch hay,
barley, and rye were grown for animal feed. At the same time,
although the college had fully vacated from Lee Hall and the old
campus, they continued to rent fields for cultivation at the Blue
Ridge farm. When the harvests from Lake Eden and Blue Ridge
were not sufficient to feed their growing—in girth and number—
live stock, the college rented plots from neighboring farmers.
Juggling multiple plots was difficult and harvest time was arduous;
it often took Penley and teams of ten or more students three days
to harvest all their corn. The work was hard but rewarding. Ruth
Lyford Sussler, a summer session student in 1944, recalled the
process of cutting cornstalks for silage:
The flow of energy that bristled from this gathering
of souls was powerful. The day’s work swallowed
you up, carried you along in the rhythm of swinging
machetes. The whole cornstalk was cut down and
then tossed onto piles which were gathered and fed
into a grinder, sucked up and blown into the top of the
silo. The noise and dust created in this process was
enormous. The excitement and energy released in this
ritual of harvesting the corn gave magic to the hard
physical labor taking place in the hot sun, making the

tete: The Farm at Black Mountain College

el.text: work seem effortless. The importance of community
manual labor as a balance to solitary thinking and
artistic effort could be well understood. '20
Fortunately, with Molly’s outreach, the college received much-
needed outside help to harvest the silage. In late summer 1944,
the nearby orphanage let the college borrow their silage cutter. In
return, Max Penley, the farmer's son, spent three days helping the
orphanage take in their silage. Also that summer they enlisted the
brawn of seven soldiers from the 134th Field Artillery who were
convalescing at nearby Moore General Hospital. The soldiers vol-
unteered on the farm at Black Mountain College for two straight
weeks and, as Molly recalled, “really saved our lives.” '21
WHEN THE COLLEGE WAS FEMALE
Always hatching a new scheme for financial betterment, Dreier,
immediately following the move from Blue Ridge to Lake Eden,
became an “earnest, eager, and enthusiastic” advocate for develop-
ing a dairy herd. When Marshall Field III, a banker, philanthropist,
and heir to the Marshall Field department store fortune, declined
to donate money to the college, Dreier convinced Field to instead
give them a bull. “King’s Regent of Dellwood,” the bull, came to
campus in fall 1941. A few months later the college purchased two
thoroughbred Guernsey cows and bought Penley’s wife Stella’s
cow as well. By this time Dreier was so cow-crazy, he began ask-
ing donors and foundations for cattle rather than cash. When that
didn’t work out, eager to add a beef herd to the college’s growing
dairy herd, Dreier spent his own money ($815) on five Angus cattle
from Phoenixville, Pennsylvania, and had them transported down
to Black Mountain. !22
Prompted in part by Dreier’s acquisition sprees, and under
Molly’s careful leadership, Black Mountain College’s livestock
operation grew significantly. By the end of summer 1943 the college
was raising 35 cows (eight dairy cows, 25 beef cows and calves, and
two bulls), 33 pigs, and over 100 chickens, mostly from Hanchett’s
original flock. The college was also home to three horses (Lady
and Pearl, mother and daughter mares, and Derek, a colt), a flock
of nine ducks, and one pet goat raised and tended by the Dreier’s
eldest son, Ted Dreier Jr. With the farm providing the college with
all its milk and butter and most of its meat and poultry, the ani-
mals fed the BMC community and provided much-needed money.
Throughout the war, the college sold calves, cows, young pigs,
and hogs to neighbors and nearby farms. Like Nan, Norm, and the
original student farmers, Molly stressed the farm as an exciting
source of community building, a space to bring people together,
to fulfill one’s responsibility, a place to have some fun. Accordingly,
students clamored to work with her—in the classroom, in the
woodshop, and on the farm. !23
One of these students was Janet Heling. Born on Long Island,
New York, in 1925, Heling learned about Black Mountain College
through a magazine article that featured photographs of young
women and men doing farm work together. She arrived at the col-
lege to study social science in the fall of 1943. Mentored by Molly,
Janet worked as the farm sub-coordinator, scheduling teams of
students to weed and water veggie beds, harvest apples and grapes,
and hoe the cornfields. She also helped record the farm’s food pro-
duction and write up brief entries for the Black Mountain College
Community Bulletin, a periodically published newsletter for campus
and alumni. '24
During Molly’s time as farm manager, work campers turned
full-time students Jagna Braunthal and Ati Gropius had a chance
to run the college’s milking operations. Born in Germany in 1927,
Braunthal and her family fled the Nazi Germany to Austria, then
Belgium, and finally to New York in 1936. Shy but exceptionally
intelligent, with an interest in physics and chemistry, Braunthal
graduated high school early, participated in two American Friends
(Quaker) work camps, and learned how to lay stone, mix con-
crete, harvest hay, and milk cows along the way. She spent a year
at Queens College, in New York, but found it devoid of the coop-
erative spirit she enjoyed at the work camps. When she learned
about Black Mountain College’s program she quickly applied. As
leader of milking operations, each morning and evening at five,
Braunthal walked ten minutes from campus to the farm to milk the
college’s cows in the summer of 1944. !25
From there, Beate “Ati” Gropius took over. The adopted
daughter of Bauhaus founder and friend-of-the-college, Walter
Gropius and his wife, Ise, Ati, whose long, curly hair, dark eye-
brows, and ample confidence gave her a regal look, was a difficult
teenager. She recalled her youth as excruciating for her and her
parents, so when they announced in 1943 that they were sending
her to Black Mountain College work camp, she feared the worst.
“I had only seen pictures of men and women bare armed or bare
chested, working away with shovels and hammering things, and
I said, ‘Oh my God, it’s a prison reform school!” The reality, how-
ever, was much different. Within 36 hours of arriving she vowed
never to leave. !26

morning at 7:30, she collected the five-gallon pails of fresh milk,
poured them into smaller cans, and placed some of the cans in
the pantry for breakfast, some in the kitchen for the cooks, and
some in a refrigerator for BMCers, including for families with
young children. Each night at 6:15 she repeated the process and
also skimmed the milk for cream and, later, butter. 127
One evening Elsa Kahl, who taught eukinetics, a course on
body conditioning and dramatic movement, entered the kitchen
and asked Ati for some skimmed milk fat to make fresh butter.
Kahl’s butter was an instant sensation. Everyone who tried it
wanted more. “The rhythm of it seems to appeal to her eukinetic
self,” literature professor Kenneth Kurtz waxed. But there was
a catch. To get more butter, they would have to make less cream.
And so, like most decisions at Black Mountain College, it was
settled at a general meeting.
A small group of two or three argued against skimming the
milk for fat to make butter, preferring whole milk for their morn-
ing coffee. Practically everyone else at the college was on board
for more butter, resting their case, it seems, entirely on the quality
of the stuff that Kahl had whipped up. In what may have been the
fastest reached consensus in Black Mountain College history, it was
decided “to have partially skimmed milk and homemade butter
instead of full milk and no butter.” Within a few weeks Black Moun-
tain College was producing 15 lb of butter a week. Unfortunately,
not all of it had been whipped by Kahl’s magic hands, 128
MOLLY GREGORY
BUILDS
Molly Gregory spent much of the war years building a new farm,
beginning with a milking house. As the college became serious
about developing a dairy herd, Molly visited the Swannanoa Test
Farm, surveyed their milking operations, and returned with a
basic plan (a “government pamphlet type of thing”) for a milking
house. She tasked Charlie and Parley to build it and asked student
Gisela Kronenberg to wire it. '29
Born in Germany in 1922, Gisela and her family fled the
Nazis in 1935 and settled in Cincinnati, Ohio. Drawn to Black
Mountain College because she liked that students could select their
own classes, Gisela arrived in fall 1940, studied psychology, and
graduated within three years. A sharp, diligent student, she loved
working with Bas Allen and threw herself into installing electricity,
putting in subflooring, building up walls, and doing masonry work.

el.text: After working extensively on the Studies Building, wiring the
milking house was easy; she finished within a few days. 130
In the summer of 1942, as both the college’s livestock and
their need for feed grew, Molly and Morton “Mort” Steinau, the
college's assistant treasurer, researched various corn silos and their
costs. They worked closely with Albers, by this time the college’s
unofficial landscape architect, who surveyed the farm and declared
the best location for the silos. Molly delegated the building of the
silos to Charlie, Mundy, and two students—Nancy West, a drama
student from Hartford, Connecticut, and Zoya Sandomirsky,
a summer student. '3!
A year earlier, Zoya and her family had escaped war-torn
Europe and landed in Chicago. Traumatized by the war, she felt
like an outsider, “a total social and emotional misfit.” Zoya enrolled
in a high school but quickly dropped out. Without a high school
diploma, she managed to be admitted to the University of Chicago
but was reluctant to attend. A friend of her mother’s suggested
Black Mountain College and convinced her to try it out during
a summer session. Surrounded by other refugees, including the
Alberses, musicologist Heinrich Jalowetz, and especially Frances
de Graaff, who taught languages and Russian history and regularly
took time to check in with the young transplant, Zoya began to
heal. She particularly relished building the silos, which “helped to
satisfy my longing for a communal, socialist experience.” During
the final stages of the project, H. G. Moffat, from the Pomona Terra
Cotta Company, joined the college to direct the tiling of the silos.
Moffat was so impressed with Black Mountain College’s can-do
spirit that he donated $5 on his way out. '32
On a bit of a building streak, Molly turned her attention to
their farm machinery, which, by the early 1940s, included a Hough
Loader tractor, flatbed farm truck, Fresno scraper, disk plow, wheat
drill, and bush and bog harrow. To house all of this a machinery
shed was built—and still exists—which is 20 ft wide by 60 ft long.
It was constructed entirely out of campus lumber and could store
equipment and machinery on one side and up to 1,200 bushels of
corn on the other. 195
The summer of 1943 saw Molly design and build three more
farm structures. After Guernsey bull King’s Regent of Dellwood
and Black Burgess, a registered Angus bull, got into a nasty fight,
separate pens and strong fences were immediately required.
She and Bas hastily designed a new bullpen and enlisted work
campers to chop endless wood to make over 300 stakes for the
pen’s fence. Bas and Pearson Mundy, who by now was working
for the college rather than for Charlie, handled the construction.

The corn silos, built by staff members Charlie Godfrey and Pearson Mundy and students
Zoya Sandomirsky and Nancy West with tiles from the Pomona Terra Cotta Company,
helped Black Mountain College feed their growing number of livestock.
Within two weeks a giant pen fit to separate a pair of warring bulls
was built. “As solid as the Rock of Gibraltar,” is how Molly described
it, “and Mundy and Bas are frightfully proud.” The only casualty
of the bullpen’s construction was Molly’s good standing with the
Board of Fellows. Opting for swift action after the fight, she’d gone
ahead without asking their permission. “I got in the doghouse with
the Board of Fellows,” she recalled, a flareup that would escalate
then defuse over the next year. 194
With the bullpen complete, Molly focused on building a new
hogpen, a task the college had been avoiding for years. For nearly
a decade Nat’s pens—built at Blue Ridge in 1934 and carted, piece by
piece, to Lake Eden in the late 1930s—had suited the college’s por-
cine needs. But as the hogs grew in size and number, a new pen was
needed. Construction began during the first week of August 1943,
with students cutting, splitting, and hauling 200 stakes for the fence.
The next week a work crew dug holes, set the stakes, and strung
wire to form the fence. Molly designed the hoghouse and built
it entirely in the woodshop, constructing six-foot prefabricated
sections, lugging the pieces to the farm, and assembling them in
situ. By the end of the month, the new hogpen was complete. To
celebrate, work campers and summer students joined Molly and
Penley for a Friday-night hayride in the farm wagon, driven by
Lady and Pearl. Leisurely they rode from Lake Eden to downtown
Black Mountain, square danced in the town square, and returned to
campus by midnight. While all the humans were relieved the hog-
pen was complete, the hogs were positively thrilled. “The pigs are
happily rooting and snorting,” wrote Molly in a Community Bulletin.
“They have been waiting for this experience for two years.” 195
The third farm structure built during the summer of 1943
was the henhouse. When Bill Hanchett left the college for the Air
Force in spring 1942, it was unclear who would tend to the 250
chicks, or “Bill’s babies” as they were known. For the next year the
chickens had been housed in “a rather questionable shanty,” accord-
ing to Molly, behind the barn. Their plight improved, sort of,
during the summer of 1943 thanks to work camper Harold Yanagi.
Born in Honolulu, Hawaii, in 1920, Yanagi studied architecture
at the Universities of Hawaii, Michigan, and at Cornell, before
graduating from the Illinois Institute of Technology. Looking to
continue his design studies and get hands-on experience, Yanagi
came to BMC hoping to study with Kocher. When he arrived at
Lake Eden, he learned that the beloved architecture professor had
taken a leave of absence, followed by his resignation. Disappointed,
Yanagi rallied and got involved in the building of the bullpen, then
jumped at the chance to build the henhouse. Like the hoghouse,

in it, electing instead to sleep and brood in the nearby trees. Stung
by the chickens’ ingratitude and disappointed in their paltry egg
