The final and most controversial farm building constructed
during the wartime summer of 1943 was the beef shed. By then the
college’s beef herd had grown considerably, resulting in cramped
quarters in the barn. That fall Molly tasked Bas and Mundy with
building a beef shed directly attached to one side of the barn. Work
crews cut down campus trees, chopped them into logs, and hauled
them to the nearby Morris Saw Mill to make lumber. By February
1944, the Board of Fellows, learning that the beef shed was over
budget, and still smarting from Molly’s unauthorized bullpen proj-
ect, halted the project and hauled Molly into a meeting. When, they
wanted to know, did we turn into a farm school? 137
To settle the bad blood, Molly organized a field trip for
board members to the farm where she reviewed two years’ worth
of building. Next, she led a general meeting for the larger campus
community to explain the past, present, and future of the farm. A
peacemaker extraordinaire, Molly reminded the community of its
goal of self-sufficiency, highlighted the vital contributions of so
many BMC members, and reassured everyone that the beef shed
would be the last new farm building until the war was over. Her
strategy worked: the board acquiesced and construction resumed. '28
RAISING THE ROOF
Beginning in 1944, the previously reliable Penley became less and
less so. When he suddenly left to work at the Morgan Manufacturing
Company, the college hired Roger Banks, a 19-year-old farmer from
Warren Wilson Junior College (formerly the Asheville Farm School).
It was a disaster. Molly persuaded Penley to return; Penley and
Banks didn’t get along; Banks left. Penley remained, semi-com-
mitted and semi-sober. George Zabriskie, who taught writing and
poetry at BMC during the 1944-45 school year, recalled Penley
drunk on moonshine, “plow[ing] fields at night, wasting precious
gasoline during wartime, and keeping people awake.” By March
1946, after Penley had left, returned, and left again, the college had
had enough. Molly—already a full-time faculty member, woodshop
supervisor, and farm manager—became head farmer. She could
swing it, she said, but not for long. '99
Truth be told, Molly was exhausted. She loved Black
Mountain College but was growing increasingly weary of the con-
stant faculty fights. As Duberman wrote: “Slice Black Mountain
open at almost any point in its history and a comparable set of
grievances, complaints, and animosities can be found.” The bat-
tles were often about policy, more often personal, and always about
power. They simmered for a year or two and boiled over every
three or four years. Although the battlelines were seldom clearly
drawn, they usually included older, long-term faculty like Josef
Albers and Ted Dreier on one side, and younger, newer faculty on
the other. The outcome was always the same: a handful of faculty
and a dozen or so loyal students would angrily leave or resign,
plunging the college into deeper instability and, worse, depriving
it of a new generation of ideas. In 1944, for example, five professors
and 20 students left the college, over the speed—or lack thereof—
of the college’s racial integration efforts, the misogynist treatment

was emerging between a young psychology professor named John
Wallen—who sought to make the Work Program more efficient
by drawing up detailed diagrams, lists, and tables and schedul-
ing meetings, committees, and more committees—and Albers and
Dreier, who wanted to keep things as they were. The battles were
brutal and traumatic. 140
For two months Molly reached out to her broad network
to find a suitable farmer for the college. Ultimately, at Dreier’s
behest, Molly contacted Raymond “Ray” Trayer, who was working
on a state farm, and whose wife Dorothy was a former student.
As it happened, not only were Ray and Dorothy Trayer interested,
but so was Ray’s farmer friend, Clifford “Cliff” Moles, and his wife
Shirley. While the college was generally excited to land not one
but two farmer families, they faced a daunting question: Where will
they live? The farmhouse, empty since Penley’s sudden departure,
was only built for a single family. '4!
The solution, Molly decided, was to raise the roof. She
would take the farmhouse’s sloping roof and raise it 45 degrees,
creating full-sized rooms where previously there was only attic
space. She enlisted help from her woodworking students, includ-
ing two future bright lights of the art world, Ruth Asawa and
Ray Johnson. Though Molly was most helped by student Miriam
“Mim” Sihvonen. Born in 1919 on Long Island and raised on a
poultry farm in Connecticut, Mim studied nursing after high
school and enlisted in the army. While stationed in Paris, she
read Adamic’s “Education on a Mountain” in Reader's Digest and
was attracted to the college’s communal living. She arrived on
campus in the spring of 1947. Although Mim intended to study
writing, she immediately gravitated toward the Work Program
and eventually took charge of it. An experienced amateur carpen-
ter, she spent most of spring semester working with Molly to
raise the roof of the farmhouse. '42
“A dream of spacious, well-planned comfort,” was how
Evarts described the new farmhouse. While functional, it was also
original, even fanciful. “It was a very funny project,” recalled Ilya
Bolotowsky, an abstract painter who taught art at the college from
1946 to 1948, and who often visited the farm to witness progress
on the roof raising. “I’m sure it was never done before—improvised
very well. It looks as it might as well take off and fly— whoop!” 143

Having trained supervisors for the woodshop having found not
one but two new farmers, and having transformed the farmhouse,
Molly Gregory was ready to leave Black Mountain College, which
she did in the summer of 1947. For her next five-year plan she
traveled north to Woodstock, Vermont, to become manager and
designer at Woodstock Enterprises, owned by original BMC stu-
dent Dave Bailey. Here Molly oversaw a woodworking shop that
first produced custom furniture and later built private homes. By
1953 she was managing two all-male crews of ten housebuilders.
She left Woodstock in 1954, and her next five-year plan lasted for
34 years. From 1954 to 1988, when she retired at age 74, Molly ran
her own custom woodworking shop in Lexington, then Lincoln,
Massachusetts, specializing in design and construction of homes,
kitchens, furniture, and an occasional henhouse. “T wanted to do
every job myself, all of it,” she told Edward S. Cooke Jt, a profes-
sor of American decorative arts at Yale, “savoring the appropriate-
ness or uniqueness of each assignment.” During this time, she also
taught woodworking, painting, scenery making, and other crafts
at Concord Academy. '44
One of Molly’s last Black Mountain College-related activities
was at a small college reunion in Lenox, Massachusetts, in 1972.
Organized by student Larry Fox and inspired by the release of
Duberman’s Black Mountain, the first published history of the col-
lege, the reunion included about 30 BMC alumni brought together
for two days and one night at a Jesuit monastery. On the first day,
many attendees, including Ati Gropius, expressed disappointment
that Molly wasn’t there. So at around six in the evening during
cocktail hour, Ati called Molly.
Ati: Are you coming?
Molly: I have to plant my peas.
Ati: Are you coming?
Molly: I have to get a cow sitter.
Ati: Coward.
Molly: I’m coming.
And she did. After finding a cow and chicken sitter, Molly hopped
in her car with her dog Grisselda and drove from Lincoln to
Lenox. She arrived at midnight to a near fully awake reunion
shrieking “Molly!” 145

From an early age Raymond “Ray” Trayer considered himself a
pacifist. Born in 1916 in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, he was raised
as a member of the Fourth Reformed Church of Christ but was
repeatedly drawn to the Quakers and their long history of pac-
ifism. In high school Ray participated in two American Friends
Service Committee work camps, including one on a co-op farm
in the Mississippi Delta. After high school he studied philoso-
phy and religion at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster,
Pennsylvania, and graduated Phi Beta Kappa in 1940. Shortly
after marrying Dorothy “Dottie” Coldren, Ray was drafted. Citing
his religion and pacifism, he declared himself a conscientious
objector. After bouncing around multiple Civilian Public Service
(CPS) camps, Ray eventually landed for two years in Ames at the
Agricultural Experiment Station of Iowa State College. There he
studied basic farming and conducted rudimentary experiments
in soils and agronomy, often under the supervision of experienced
farmer Clifford “Cliff” Moles. 146
Cliff Moles was born in 1920 and raised on a farm near
Shenandoah, Iowa. Kind and hard-working, Moles and his father
operated two well-respected local farms. 1942 was a big year for
Moles. He married Shirley McWhorter, got drafted, and, citing
his religion (Methodist) and pacificism, declared himself a con-
scientious objector. Moles was stationed at a CPS camp in Elmira,
New York, moved on to manage the farm for a mental hospital in
Concord, New Hampshire, and finally settled for two and a half
years at the Agricultural Experiment Station (AES). A keen farmer
and organizer, Moles was named farm manager of the Howard
County Experimental Farm, an AES satellite in the northeast cor-
ner of Iowa, where he enjoyed freedom to carry out experimental
agricultural techniques. '47
With Ray and Cliff finding common ground while at work in
the fields, in the evenings of 1944 the Trayers and the Moleses often
met for dinner. There was plenty of talk about farming and paci-
ficism, but invariably the highlight was Dottie’s stories about her
nine months at a small, experimental school called Black Mountain
College. Dottie had graduated high school first in her class at age
16 and then trained as a lab technician. Now she worked in bacteri-
ology at Iowa State College’s Veterinary Hygiene Department. But
before that she had attended BMC to study piano under Frederic
“Fritz” Cohen, composer, music professor, and husband to Elsa
Kahl, butter master. Within months Dottie had joined the staff, first
as college registrar and later as assistant treasurer. Over dinner in
Ames she regaled the three others with stories about BMC com-
munity living, about general meetings that stretched well into the

She was gleeful when she relived a Saturday night campus con-
cert where she played three pieces by Schubert. On the fields and
over dinner, the Moleses and Trayers “became quite close friends,”
recalled Cliff; he “hoped for some time we would work together
for a common purpose.” !48
Fortunately, Ray had a plan for the four of them. From
as early as November 1943, he began exchanging letters with
Dreier. Ray kept Dreier abreast of his training at the Agricultural
Experimental Station and his classes in crop production and weld-
ing taken at Iowa State College. Strategically, Ray appealed to
Dreier’s professed decade-long dream to hire a farmer who could
teach classes by littering his letters with casual mentions of agri-
cultural-related articles and books, including agronomist Edward
H. Faulkner’s 1943 book Plowman’s Folly. Finally, he regularly
enclosed a modest donation check of $5 to the college. 149
In early July 1946, Cliff, Shirley, and their two-year-old
daughter Diane arrived at Black Mountain College. Molly was pos-
itively gleeful about Cliff and “his quiet and really sound idealism.”
Two months later, Ray, Dottie, and one-year-old daughter Susan
arrived. With Molly fixing to leave, and these two families ready to
take over the farm, a new era was set to begin. 150
THE MOLES-TRAYER REGIME
Under Cliff Moles and Ray Trayer, the farm at Black Mountain
College became more orderly and organic. Moles took inventory
of anything he could count, categorize, or measure, including farm
buildings, machinery, tools, livestock, silage, and seed. He took
endless soil samples across multiple fields. He pored through past
and present farm budgets and studied the costs and returns of the
livestock. Later, he and Trayer suggested the farm reduce the beef
cattle, increase the dairy herd, and pause the pig population until
further housing could be built and additional feed could be grown.
Within a year of their arrival the farm exuded order. “They prac-
tically iron the fields after planting,” wrote Molly—who had stuck
around long enough to witness this development—in the Black
Mountain College Bulletin. “They are a mechanized pair and pretty
gay with their tractor. '51
The farm under Moles and Trayer followed a set of practices
that have come to define organic farming. The focus was on build-
ing healthy soil, so they planted endless acres of cover crops. They
established a large-scale composting operation that combined food
scraps from the kitchen, greens from the garden, and manure from
Black Mountain College farmer Clifford "Cliff" Moles on tractor, 1948.
the farm to make rich, healthy compost to add to garden beds,
fields, and orchards. Molly described the massive composting oper-
ation as “a whole village street of rectangle piles,” which Moles and
Trayer examined “with almost morbid solemnity.” Finally, they
initiated a series of soil conservation practices like contouring, ter-
racing, and, influenced by Faulkner’s Plowman’s Folly—a founda-
tional text for natural farming methods in the US—judicious use of
the plow. '52
Moles and Trayer were aided in their efforts by a number
of experienced and capable student-farmers, starting with William
“Bill” Treichler. Born in 1924 to a homesteading family living in
Cedar Rapids, Iowa, Treichler’s family grew their own food, raised
and slaughtered their own animals, and baked their own bread out
of homegrown wheat. When the war came Bill joined the Army
Air Force and was stationed in England. While there, he read The
Living Soil by Eve Balfour, a British farmer and pioneer of the
emerging organic food and farming movement, and discovered that
her experimental farm was within cycling distance from his air-
base. He became a regular visitor and Balfour ordered books for the
eager young farmer. Upon returning to Iowa, Treichler found his
family obsessed with “decentralism,” a rejection of industrialism,

campus timber.

urbanism, and consumerism and embrace of self-sufficiency, family-
scale economies, and community cooperation. Together the
family attended homesteading conferences organized by decen-
tralist writer Mildred Loomis, and it was in Milton Wend’s How to
Live in the Country Without Farming that Treichler’s mom found
Black Mountain College in a list of colleges to which homesteading
parents should send their children. 153
Arriving at Black Mountain College with his parents in late
summer 1947, Treichler, who had high standards when it came to
landscaping, was horrified by the lack of campus upkeep. While the
farm had been taken over by trusted hands, the Work Program was
in disarray and the campus had begun to flounder—a sign of things
to come. “The school entrance looked weedy and the grounds
were grown up with long grass,” Treichler recalled. “The property
looked ignored and neglected.” After a full day of walking around
campus, looking into buildings, touring the farm, and meeting with
new writing professor, lauded poet and, later, potter M. C. (Mary
Caroline) Richards, Treichler remained stunned by the school’s
appearance and wanted to drive back to Iowa. “You should give the
place a try,” his parents said reassuringly. “Maybe you can cut the
grass and weeds.” Treichler relented. '54
And cut grass and weeds he did. Within days, Treichler
connected with Moles and Trayer who gave him access to the trac-
tor to use all over the campus, especially along its roads and around
its buildings. Albers was impressed by Treichler’s efforts and, from
his unofficial role as campus landscaper, gave him carte blanche
on landscaping matters. Within weeks Treichler was entrusted to
lead multiple farming operations and within months he became
the college’s Work Program coordinator. During his time at BMC
he would deepen his understanding of organic farming, in part
due to the teachings of chemistry and physics professor Natasha
Goldowski, a world expert on corrosive chemistry. Born in Moscow
and trained in Paris, Goldowski had been a member of the US gov-
ernment’s top-secret Manhattan Project, which created the first
atomic bomb. '55
During the first week of his second year at BMC, Treichler
met Martha Rittenhouse, a new student from a farm in Maryland,
who shared his interest in homesteading. Under the supportive
watch of librarian Nell Rice, Bill courted Martha in the college
library. He invited her to read and discuss—who else?—Ralph
Borsodi. They began with Borsodi’s first book, Education and Living,
continued with Flight from the City, and by the time they got to his
most recent book, This Ugly Civilization, they were going steady.
Later that year the duo invited Borsodi to visit Black Mountain

Another essential student-farmer was Ruth Aiko Asawa.
Born in 1926 in Norwalk, California, Asawa came from a farming
family. Because of California’s discriminatory laws against “aliens”
including those of Asian descent, Asawa’s father, Umakichi, and
mother, Haru, were unable to own land. Instead they leased a whom
ping 85 acres spread across three parcels where they and their
seven children grew vegetables and fruit, loaded it up on a truck.
and sold it at markets in nearby Los Angeles. As a child, Asawa
worked before and after school on the family farm, all year round.
growing cabbage, cauliflower, and parsnips in the winter, carrots
and strawberries in the spring, and melons and tomatoes in the
summer. The work was grueling for Asawa and her siblings and
only ceased on Saturdays, when they attended Japanese school and
where Asawa learned calligraphy, and for a few hours on Sundays,
when they went to the Quaker church, the only house of worship in
the area that welcomed Japanese Americans. 157
With the bombing of Pearl Harbor in December 194], the
Asawa family’s hard life grew harder. Within two months, without
warning, FBI agents appeared at the farm and took Umakichi away
to an undisclosed location. Asawa and her family would not see
him for the next six years. Two months after her father had been
arrested, Asawa, her mother and five of her siblings were told to
report to the Santa Anita racetrack where they would live in horse
stables for the next five months. Conditions were hideous: horsehair
covered the walls; the smell of horse was constant and, especially
on hot days, overbearing; their bath, toilet, and laundry were public.
Despite this Asawa blossomed as an artist, taking makeshift
painting classes with fellow internees Tom Okamoto, Ben Tanaka,
and Chris Ishii, artists and illustrators from Disney Studios. “He got
us drawing,” she recalled about Okamoto, “and we posed for each
other.” After five months the Asawas were transferred to Rohwer
Relocation Center in Arkansas, where they supplemented their mis-
erable meals with fresh vegetables planted near their “apartment”
(Block 13-11-A) from seeds Haru saved from the farm. Through all
of this, Asawa found solace in painting and drawing classes, and in
leading a letter-writing campaign with her siblings and Edythe
Byars, a Quaker from Norwalk, to request the release of her father.
Although the war wouldn’t end until 1945, the US govern-
ment established prewar releases for internees who were high
school graduates—if they signed a loyalty statement, enrolled
in a Midwest college (the coasts being military zones), and secured

Service Committee. They traveled to Toluca, a town outside
Mexico City, where Asawa taught children to draw. The summer
was filled with adventures, including multiple visits from Josef

TEACHING AND TENSIONS
After spending fall semester getting familiar with their new
home, Moles and Trayer developed Black Mountain College’s
first farm-related course in spring 1947. Although teaching had
occurred on the farm from the start, including Bas Allen’s prun-
ing lessons and student-led workshops, the lessons were always
informal and separate from the college’s official curriculum.
This changed with Moles and Trayer’s Getting Acquainted with
Agriculture (universally referred to as Farming), a hybrid class,
part seminar, part practice, which offered students “first-hand
knowledge and experience of the operations of a small general
farm.” Students read books like Plowman’s Folly and J. I. Rodale’s
Pay Dirt: Farming and Gardening with Composts. These and cur-
rent farming topics were discussed with a passionate Trayer and
a more reluctant Moles during once-a-week evening seminars.
Each student was expected to maintain a farm project, like milking
cows, raising rabbits, starting a beehive, or repairing the tractor.
The class attracted a modest seven students. Two of them, Verna
Raattama and Katherine “Sue” Schauffler, excelled. The rest flailed.
One student, Richard “Dick” Sherman, worked hard on the farm
but “never worked up a tremendous enthusiasm for the course.”
Another, Howard Rondthaler, son of faculty member Theodore
Rondthaler, participated regularly in the seminar, but never once
set foot on the farm. '62
The seminar exposed a tension between the farmers. Moles
found Trayer’s knowledge of the issues at hand to be intellectual
but inexperienced and found his professorial tone pompous. He
was also turned off by Trayer’s ambitious nature. For example,
in spring 1947 when the college found itself short on faculty and
lacking a quorum, the board of faculty invited Moles and Trayer
to join. Trayer, perhaps seeing it as a way to advance, accepted
immediately. Moles mulled it over. It was not that Moles was
detached from the college. He taught, ate meals in the dining room,
and attended college parties with his family. Further, he was often
relied on in general meetings as a de-escalating mediator when
things got hot. But Moles did not consider himself a teacher, much
less a college professor. After a couple of weeks of consternation,
Moles reluctantly accepted. '6$
Discord also rose from the farmers’ dissimilar farm experi-
ence. While Moles was born and raised on a farm and had managed
farms throughout his conscientious objector service, Trayer was
new to it, a farming student to be more accurate. “He didn’t have
any previous farming experience,” Shirley Moles recalled. “He had
read about it and wanted to do it.” Oftentimes, Moles would sug-
gest a routine task to Trayer and instead of asking questions, Trayer
would flounder and, feeling insecure, get upset. Despite this and
to Moles’s great frustration, Trayer had stealthily assumed the role
of farm manager to Moles’ assistant farm manager. He partici-
pated more actively with the faculty, which it seems had led some
members of the community to consider him more knowledgeable.
Acrimony further flared, no doubt, with both farmers and their
families living under one roof. '64
By spring 1948, perhaps as a way to cool tempers, the farm-
ers decided to teach two separate classes. Moles taught Farming,
while Trayer developed a new class called Soil and Steel. The
aggrandized course summary gives weight to Moles’s accusation
of Trayer as high-minded. Soil and Steel was “a study of the farmer
and the industrial worker; nature of the social and economic set-
ting; physical and psychological wants and needs of both groups;
background of the labor movement; major problems of labor; mod-
ern agricultural patterns; the interdependence of the farmer and
wage earner; techniques toward unity. Two hours weekly.” The
highlight of the course was a two-week-long field trip to visit var-
ious government dams built across North Carolina and Tennessee.
Despite initial student interest—25 students signed up—the class
tanked. Only one student, Albert Lanier, managed to complete
a final research paper. Trayer’s brutal assessment of the students
did not help the situation. He accused them of limited intelligence,
poor analytical skills, and over-emotionalism. One unfortunate
student, Wilma Fuerstenberg was said by Trayer to do “little more,
seemingly, than occupy space.” 165
By summer 1948 patience had worn thin. That summer,
neighboring cattle trespassed through subpar fencing to munch on

the next-door farmer. The second time the cattle invaded, Moles

collected the cows and herded them home. While still at the neigh-

FEUDING CAMPUS
While the college was no stranger to protracted power struggles,
the biggest of them all began in summer 1948 and peaked a year
later. On one side was Theodore “Ted” Rondthaler (history, college
treasurer from 1945-48), Albert William “Bill” Levi (social sci-
ences, current rector), and M. C. Richards (English, married to but
not in lockstep with Levi). It is difficult to think of a more differ-
ent BMC couple than M. C. and Levi. Levi was intellectual, erudite,
and pedantic. He taught sociology at Dartmouth College and the
University of Chicago before coming, with M. C., both in their late
twenties, to Black Mountain College to teach philosophy in 1945. As
a teacher, Levi, bald, serious, and a bit chilly, was formal, especially
for informal BMC, and, as Duberman wrote, “tended to lecture and,
even off the platform, to pontificate—to hand down truths.” As a
person he was cagey. Few faculty trusted him. As rector, which he
took over from Dreier in spring 1947, his focus was on building up
the humanities and social sciences, fields that Albers had been
hostile toward, widening the rift between the two. '68
While M. C. held many similar beliefs, especially regard-
ing the primacy of the humanities and social sciences within the
curriculum, she carried herself in an altogether different way.
Young, warm, attractive, and friendly, M. C., now considered one
of the shining lights of Black Mountain College, came from the
University of Chicago and University of California, Berkeley, in
search of a less standardized pedagogy. She taught a half dozen
classes, all categorized under “Reading” or “Writing,” and ran
them the way John Andrew Rice had done (minus the bullying).
In class, students and professor would spend hours getting to the
bottom ofa text as well as their individual beliefs. “M. C. wanted
you to find yourself,” said poetry student Joel Oppenheimer. She
embraced the communal spirit of the college and quickly became,
with a few exceptions, one of BMC’s favorite teachers and mem-
bers of the community. Beyond the classroom, M. C. and a reluc-
tant Levi often hosted students at their cottage where they would
read poetry, discuss literature, and feast on M. C.’s homemade
blackberry pie. 169
On the other side, once again, were Albers and Dreier. Tired
of new professors offering ideas on how to run the college and, in
Albers’ words, “this constant over-democratic nonsense,” he and
Dreier proposed hiring new faculty on a one-year visiting basis,
with neither voting rights nor admittance to the Board of Fellows.
Levi, M. C., and Rondthaler were appalled. What’s more, perhaps
feeling underappreciated for their contributions to the college over
the past decade and a half, Albers and Dreier proposed changing
faculty salaries from need-based to seniority-based, which would
benefit them, the college’s most senior faculty. Levi et al. were
aghast. In a move that would have shocked Rice in his founding
vow to avoid administrative strangleholds, Albers and Dreier pro-
posed decreasing the power of the faculty, increasing the power
of the rector, and creating an outside board of trustees. Levi, M. C.,
and Rondthaler were horrified. '7°
Sadly, students were not immune to the power grab. First,
Albers sought to change the nomination process for student rep-
resentatives; nominations were to come from faculty instead of
the students themselves. Second, Albers demanded eliminating
the practice of students teaching courses. A year earlier while he
and Anni were on sabbatical in Mexico, the college allowed three
advanced students—Harry Holl (sculpture), Arthur Penn (acting),
and Jimmie Tite (printing)—to develop courses. By the time Albers
had returned and fall semester was underway, Holl had repur-
posed an old tool shed into a forging and sculpture shed, created
an introductory sculpture studio class, and was currently teaching
eight students. '7!
Albers was livid. His fury was aimed at Holl in particu-
lar, who, a year earlier, had dropped Albers’ course after only a
few sessions. One day, Albers tracked Holl down on campus and
demanded he stop teaching. The class, explained Albers, should
have been approved by him, the head of art. Holl thought it over
and replied, “I am going to go on with the course.”
Stunned, Albers eventually recovered, smiled, and invited
Holl to tea at his faculty cottage. Over tea and pumpernickel,
brought in from New York, the professor told the student the rea-
sons why he should not, could not, and would not teach this class.
Holl, older than most students, having spent three years in the
service, was neither intimidated nor impressed. “I’m teaching
the class.”
Albers, “a little shaky and angry,” said he wouldn't allow it.
Holl, who was on the GI Bill, which funded returning
servicepeople in education, explained that if he must stop teach-
ing the course, then he would need to report to Veteran Affairs in
Asheville that his recently approved student-teacher status had
to be changed to full-time student status; thereby disrupting his
year-long course of study, which meant the college would need
to return Holl’s GI funds, and that would trigger an automatic
reevaluation of Black Mountain College’s accreditation as a GI Bill
institution. GI Bill money was steady income for the college and
the older professor knew it. Checkmated, Albers seethed and pro-
ceeded to ignore Holl throughout the remainder of the student's
stay at the college. 172
Predictably, faculty meetings were toxic. Camps formed and
conversations quickly descended into name calling. Old schoolers
Albers and Dreier labeled newer faculty M. C. and Levi as transients,
unable or unwilling to appreciate the college’s history. In turn, new

be arts and music—no more history or math—supplemented by

by visiting (i.e. no voting privileges) faculty. Second, in mid-De-

this time in New York City. '76
Back on campus, Trayer convened a meeting of his own.
This time, Dreier was under fire. Four other Board of Fellows mem-

Trayer in lambasting Dreier, bringing into serious question the
longstanding faculty member’s fitness. Although Dreier had always
raised eyebrows for his barreling nature, idealization of physi-

vicious. Librarian Rice was furious with Dreier for his support of
hiring new faculty without voting privileges. Goldowski was livid
at Dreier for his recent public shaming of a student couple who
were caught spending the night together, and his attempt to expel
the female student. Trayer’s list of grievances was long. He railed
against Dreier’s habit of visiting the farm with a list of “urgent”
tasks only to change the list the next day. He complained about
Dreier’s impulsive decisions, like when he bought a litter of piglets
for the farm with no consideration of where they would be housed,
how they would be fed, and who would care for them. He fulmi-
nated against Dreier’s support of an outside board of trustees, and
reintroduced a stale rumor that Dreier was trying to sell the col-
lege to the University of North Carolina. Worse, Trayer concluded,
Dreier was having an open affair with a faculty member, bringing
shame to both Bobbie and the college and bringing pain to him
personally as a Quaker. By the end of the meeting the five members,
constituting a bare quorum, voted to demand that Dreier resign
from Black Mountain College. '77

January 1949, Nell Rice, acting as spokesperson for the Board of
Fellows, informed him that they had decided he must resign from
the college. Dreier was stunned. He asked Nell for the decision

was presented with a petition later that day signed by more than
half of the students—perhaps seizing the moment—asking him to
resign as a teacher of mathematics. That night Dreier made his
way to the barn, no doubt looking for peace. There, “right into the

FACULTY MEETING FIGHT
During his three-month stint as interim rector, Trayer kept
a few balls in the air, including helping visiting faculty member
Buckminster Fuller organize the forthcoming Summer Institute,
corresponding with more than 50 students who had signed up
for the Institute, and retaining poet-pedagogue Charles Olson,
who would become a key BMC figure in the coming years. '8!
Over the 1949-50 school year, within a climate of suspicion
and indecision, the college faculty and other leaders did their best to
keep heads above water. Without Josef Albers to protest, the college
hired two new social science professors, Paul Leser (anthropology)
and Flola Shepard (linguistics); three advanced students (Hazel
Larsen Archer, Joseph Fiore, and Pete Jennerjahn) to teach visual
arts; and one student (Betty Jennerjahn) to teach dance. The college
also hired a handful of Quakers, including Robert Turner to begin a
ceramics program, John McCandless to run the printshop, Vollmer
Hetherington to teach music appreciation, Louise Hetherington
to teach piano, and Don Warrington to serve as treasurer. Following

Although the college was functional, the atmosphere was
far from amicable, and soon another intra-faculty battle began
to brew. While the battlelines were fluid, they roughly fell into
two camps: the Quakers argued for a more conventional and
conservative college, while Levi, M. C., and most of the students
advocated for a more bohemian one, in line with the college’s
past. This rift was especially apparent when the faculty discussed
visiting professor Paul Goodman. '83
BMC was still attracting acclaimed names, and Goodman
arrived at Black Mountain College as part of a diverse group of vis-
iting professors that included sculptor Leo Amino, critic Clement
Greenberg, dancer Katherine Litz, and artist Theodoros Stamos. A
writer, social critic, psychoanalyst, and, in the decade that followed,
guru to the counterculture, Goodman was hired to teach writing
but brought so much more. “The guy was loaded with guns,” stu-
dent Fielding “Fee” Dawson wrote much later. “He came down with
psychotherapy (his own), literature, history, community planning,
and sex.” While few questioned his teaching skills, some members
of the community were disturbed (or threatened) by his open bisex-
uality. Goodman’s flirtations didn’t help. As Mary Emma Harris
wrote, he was “aggressive in his pursuit of young men, and students
who had been pursued by Goodman were tired of having to deal
constantly with his advances.” 184
When Goodman requested to stay longer to teach, a hiring
process kicked in that included a series of meetings. At one, Trayer,
acting as the Quakers’ spokesperson, expressed fear that Goodman
would sexually assault the faculty’s children. “Why does everyone
think Paul wants your 13-year-old boy,” a meeting attendee asked
sarcastically, “when there are all these groovy 20-year-olds around?”
Later, Trayer accused Goodman of public indecency when, during
a campus softball game, he urinated behind a tree in the outfield
rather than walk a quarter mile to the bathroom. Joel Oppenheimer,
a poetry student from New York, retorted: “Everyone has peed
behind that tree!” 185
Four years after his arrival, pacifist Trayer had become
hostile and violent, leading many to doubt his emotional stability.
One student, Edward Stanley “Stan” Vanderbeek, had a particu-
larly disturbing relationship with Trayer. Initially Vanderbeek
was eager to work with the antiwar farmer. “I was very seriously
involved in [being a] conscientious objector and the belief in it,
and all those struggles you do for moral value:” But Trayer disap-
pointed Vanderbeek with his violent behavior. He would “beat up
a cow any chance he had. I mean he was just furious at them; if they
disobeyed him, he was just an absolute militarist.” Another student,
Harry Weitzer, recalled a day on the farm when Trayer was bitten
by Pearl, the horse. “Ray was furious,” wrote Weitzer. “He pulled
that horse’s head down and took hold of her ear in his own mouth.
The horse stood still as Lot’s wife. When the battle was clearly over,
Ray straightened up and spit a neat semicircle of ear.” 186

six months later Trayer had taken on the role of farm manager

ing chair all day, too injured to work, too poor to quit. Regardless of
the reasons why, few students and fewer professors showed up for
their weekly shifts. Some students resented the program altogether
and refused to participate. Art student John Chamberlain, for
example, “loathed the community scene,” recalled Creeley, calling
it “some great banal boy scout scene.” 193
Once in a while, a meeting was called to drum up participa-
tion. “Come on, get out there with your scythe!” Baker remembered
faculty imploring. “So you're bright, you still have to have some
physical exercise!” Besides not wanting to work, few even knew
how to do the work required—the “each one, teach one” pedagogi-
cal practice that had thrived at the college throughout the 1930s
and 40s was gone. When it came to basic campus maintenance,
“no one knew how to do it,” recalled Mixon, and “no one was the
least bit interested in doing it.” 194

el.text: On a rare chance that a work crew was assembled, the
results were comical. Once, Olson managed to put together a half
dozen students to work a Saturday afternoon on the farm. Shortly
after they had started, however, Olson and art student Dan Rice
got into a heated debate that quickly escalated into a nasty argu-
ment. “Enough!” Rice announced. He turned to the crew and
offered to buy all of them, minus Olson, a beer. In sync the students
dropped their tools, about-faced, and started walking the four miles
to Ma Peak’s Tavern, a bar located outside the town limits of Black
Mountain. Abandoned, Olson yelled, “a fine lot of fish!” to the
refreshment-seeking deserters. 195
Evidence of the Work Program’s collapse was everywhere.
The lawns and fields that Treichler devotedly plowed and the roads
and pathways Albers and student crews diligently maintained were
nowhere to be found. Weeds were neck high. When a rare visitor
showed up, they had to be literally guided through campus. “Grass
and shrubs had not been cut for months,” recalled Robert Moore,
a local high school student in 1954, “so we followed the students as
they wound their way along paths through the trees and deep grass.”
Helene Dorn, who accompanied her husband Ed, a writing student,
and their young children to BMG, observed, “It was a weird sight
and easy to understand how large settlements can be buried alive
by the jungle.” 196
Campus buildings were unkempt and battered. The Studies
Building, Black Mountain College’s greatest architectural achieve-
ment, was a disaster. The foundations were shaky, the coalbin
had caved in, and broken windows were replaced with cardboard
and tape. Poet Robert Duncan, who taught at the college in spring
1956, remembered the structure as “a derelict piece of modernism,”
adding, “nothing looks more run-down than an art moderne build-
ing ten years later.” Inside, students stacked their trash—drafts
of papers, uneaten food, cigarette butts—in mounds that grew 6 ft
tall. When the mounds took over their studies, the students simply
moved to a new study. The library, once a jewel, was shot—its
front door no longer closed, its books were moldy and often pil-
fered. When faculty and students left, “they just stole the damned
books,” recalled secretary Baker, “just walked away with them,
volumes, collector’s items and art books from Europe, you know,
magnificent things.” 197
Other buildings were closed or abandoned. The pot shop
was padlocked. The woodshop was leased to student Don Mixon,
who seldom used it and never paid rent. The printshop was barely
functional and “leaves littered the type cases,” wrote Olson biogra-
pher Tom Clark. One faculty cottage was relinquished as it slowly
slid off its foundations and down the mountain. The glass-and-
metal Science Building was abandoned. Duncan recalled finding
“deserted laboratories with broken glass, and splendid kiln equip-
ment which had just gone to ruin.” Kudzu, a fast-growing vine, grew
up, around, and over North and South Lodges and all the faculty
cottages. The farmhouse was vacant. In the Round House, a once
“fantastic collection of records” was scattered across the floor; some
unsleeved LPs rested on tables through the hot summer until they
melted, Dali-esque, down the edges. By 1955, “Black Mountain was
only about ideas,” wrote student Martha King. “Almost everything
else had been abandoned, lost, broken, fallen in.” 198
While the plant eroded, campus services became practically
non-existent. Gone were the days when earnest, hard-working
crews loaded coal from the train station in Black Mountain and
hauled it back to campus. Instead, a small heap of damp, soft coal
was occasionally delivered to the doorsteps of some faculty cot-
tages. Lumber was sometimes cut, rarely delivered, and never
ample. Mildred Harding, a nearly finished graduate student in
English at Columbia University, wife to anthropology professor
John Adams, and mother of a baby and toddler, recalled a horrific
winter during the 1951-52 school year. “I remember 2 a.m. bottle
feedings at just above zero indoors, huddling in layers of blankets,
the baby in my arms, buried in there, only his nostrils and lips vis-
ible.” Although meals were still served, they peaked at the begin-
ning of the month, when cooks Cornelia Williams and Malrey Few
worked within their tiny monthly budget. As the month went on
and the budget dwindled, the meals worsened. !99
Even laundry services disappeared. During summer 1953,
a German museum director visited Black Mountain College for a
few days. “After he left,” Rhodes remembered, “it was discovered
that no one had put sheets on his bed or given him towels, so he had
just been sleeping on a dirty old mattress in his room. It wasn’t any-
body’s business. And that’s the way it went.” By 1955, the college’s
last remaining washing machine, the one that had been faltering for
years, finally collapsed. Above the machine, someone posted a sign
that read: FUCKT. 200
OLSON’S UNIVERSITY
Like so many others, Charles Olson first learned about Black
Mountain College by reading Louis Adamic’s 1936 article in
Harper’s. The college’s rebellious roots and Rice’s pursuit of a
new kind of college deeply resonated with him. As Tom Clark
wrote, Olson was especially impressed with “Black Mountain’s
Art student Dan Rice and writing professor Robert “Bob" Creeley under the Studies
Building at Black Mountain College, 1955.
i Mig tats A
downplaying of traditional educational ‘solidities’ (like buildings,
credits, grades) in favor of intangible spiritual and intellectual
values.” The college’s agrarianism and communalism, however,
repelled Olson. When he read Adamic’s account of the student-run
farm, he recalled saying to himself, “Oh shit!” 201
In fall 1948, BMC hired writer Edward Dahlberg to replace
M. C. Richards, who, along with husband Levi, took a year-long
leave of absence. Within two weeks, Dahlberg, frustrated with
the college’s foliage, students, and uncivility, angrily left and sug-
gested Olson as a replacement. Olson was living in Washington, DC,
but agreed to teach intensive seminars on writing and literature,
commuting to the college for a week every month throughout the
1948-49 school year. In summer 1951, looking for some sense of
home for himself and his pregnant, common-law wife Constance
“Connie” Olson, Olson returned to the college where he remained,
more or less, until it closed in 1956, and through the next year to sell
off anything worth something, pay off debts, and close accounts.
His classes were legendary, his intellectual scope—especially in
terms of history, mythology, literature, and poetry—was extraordi-
nary, and he quickly gained followers. By all accounts, Olson was
huge—in size (approximately 6 ft 8 in. and around 280 Ib), presence,
confidence, and ego. “Charles Olson!” wrote Harding, “he seemed,
even then, at 42, half mythic: bard, guru, titan.” 202
Although Olson showed up in the classroom, he was a con-
stant no-show when it came to the Work Program. He resented
being expected to participate. As a student of the college's history,
Olson was well aware that many of BMC’s fights and flights, or
what he called, “rump revolts and jumps away,” were centered on
issues of community and physical labor. His perspective on this
type of involvement was unequivocal; “No more of this community
horseshit!” Olson wrote in 1953. 203
Initiated under Levi's rectorship and institutionalized
during Olson’s reign, contingency salaries for faculty were
intended to help the college remain afloat. These were essentially
1OUs. Faculty were paid half the amount of their previously agreed
upon salary with a promise that the other half would be paid once
the college was more financially sound. Later, as things got more
desperate, faculty were offered food from the farm, which by this
point was being run by Doyle Jones, a local farmer who had taken
over where the Trayers had left off. Faculty would get part of a pig
or a basket of beans in place of an IOU. With their hunger increas-
ing and expectation to be paid decreasing, most faculty reluctantly
accepted the food. Each year, these contingency salaries accrued
and accumulated and their fate was ultimately settled in court. 24
SAVING THE COLLEGE
While the college was surely crumbling, it was not collapsing.
Classes continued, meals were served, and modest buildings were
(slowly) built. This was due in part to farmer Doyle Jones.
A “lean, handsome man with the bluest eyes,” as described
by writing student Michael Rumaker, Jones had spent most of his
life farming the Black Mountain region and specialized in raising
livestock, especially hogs and beef cattle. He also had building skills
he had picked up through brief stints at Essex Chair Company and
the Morgan Manufacturing Company, where he worked alongside
Ross Penley, Black Mountain College’s first farmer. In early June
1951, right after the Trayers left the college, Doyle was hired as the
new farmer. The job gave him use of the fully furnished farmhouse
Doyle Jones, Black Mountain College's last farmer, spring 1952.
and access to a large garden plot, maintained mostly by Doyle’s
wife, Claire, or “Clara,” a member of the Cherokee Nation, and their
14-year-old son, Ben. 205
Doyle arrived to high expectations. After Trayer’s quick
retreat, his wife Dottie had run the farm. When that didn’t work,
the college temporarily hired art student Vanderbeek, who “hardly
knew one end of the cow from another.” By comparison Doyle
knew what he was doing with the land. He also served on college
committees, procured moonshine for students, and drove folks to
Asheville for errands. Doyle took control of the dairy herd, trained
writing and art student Terence Burns to assist him, and began
providing the college with all its milk, eggs, and butter, once again.
He regularly slaughtered members of the beef herd until one
year later, they were no more. While Doyle was experienced with
livestock, he was less adroit when it came to growing vegetables,
so although food came from the farm, it didn’t exactly flow. With
little income to count on and a reliance on food-in-kind, Harding
recalled: “As winter settled in and less and less food trickled from
farm to dining room—for one long stretch, almost nothing but
milk, eggs, and red beans—I pictured my children withered and
deformed with beriberi and scurvy.” 206
But Doyle’s underwhelming food production was arguably
impressive given the lack of resources. In the past, the farm had a
budget to purchase needed equipment, repair old tools, and initiate
new projects. Now, Doyle had such a small budget he couldn’t afford
fertilizer. In the past, the farm had an agricultural program, which
introduced basic farming skills to the wider BMC community. Now,
Doyle had none of that. In the past, the college had a functional
Work Program, a generally agreed-upon collection of practices
where all members of the college worked with staff in service to the
campus and farm. Now, Doyle had, if lucky, a handful of students
show up on the farm on Saturday afternoons. In the past, expert
community partners had been on hand to help. Now, the only com-
munity partners Doyle had were his farming friends and drinking
buddies, who sometimes came to campus to help harvest silage but
often spent their time taunting students. 297
One such instance involved writing student Michael
Rumaker. In late 1951, Rumaker was living precariously in Phila-
delphia, having recently been kicked out of his family home for
being queer. By chance, he and a friend attended a lively talk at
the Philadelphia Museum of Art by painter Ben Shahn who spoke
rapturously about an unconventional place called Black Mountain
College and its writing teacher Charles Olson. Intrigued, Rumaker
visited Mary Reed, who taught painting at the Moore Institute
of Art, and asked her thoughts. “Oh, yes, Black Mountain,” Reed
answered, “I hear it’s a hotbed of communism and homosexuals.”
Immediately Rumaker wrote a letter of inquiry to the college, not-
ing his poverty, and quickly received a reply from Connie Olson,
then BMC registrar, who touted the college’s work scholarships
and invited him to visit. Rumaker visited in the summer of 1952,
was smitten, and arrived as a student in fall 1952. 298
Upon arrival Rumaker joined a crew assisting Doyle to
complete the last stage of a weeks-long process of turning corn into
silage. Although Rumaker didn’t mind the intensive work nor the
oppressive heat, he felt demoralized by the rude snickering from
the local farmers who called the students “city slickers” and mocked
them—especially Rumaker—as unmasculine, with Doyle adding his
own two cents. The next day, Rumaker requested a transfer to the
kitchen team. 299

in Chicago in 1925, Paul Francis Williams Jr was raised by mother,
Gretchen, a smart, independent farm girl, and father, Paul, an elec-
trical engineer and inventor who amassed a huge fortune through
his company, G & W Electric Specialty Co. From kindergarten
through high school Paul Jr attended the prestigious North Shore
Country Day School, where he enjoyed woodworking and stu-
dent government and took classes from former BMC student Nat
French and future BMC history professor David Corkran. As Mark
Davenport, a music historian at Regis College, wrote, “despite
coming from a family of wealth—or perhaps as a reaction against
Paul Williams, initially a BMC student of architecture, then architect in residence, and
lastly Black Mountain College's final funder, circa 1952-53.
it—Williams developed a disdain for pretension in all its forms.”
Following high school, he enlisted in the military and spent two
years on a B-29 bomber. After completing his service Williams, was
accepted to Black Mountain College, arriving in January 1946. 2!0
Williams, like many other BMC students, yearned for archi-
tecture classes. With no architect-in-residence since Kocher’s
departure three years prior, Williams took summer classes with
Walter Gropius and later with Buckminster Fuller. Wanting more,
in the fall of 1947 Williams recruited a group of students to join
a weekly architecture seminar. With modest funding ($1,000) from
his mother, he and the seminar students designed and built the
Minimum House, a modern 400 sq ft home made of aluminum
siding, wood, glass, and rocks gathered from campus. Constructed
to prove that good design didn’t have to be pricey, the Minimum
House’s south-facing side was made primarily of glass, taking
advantage of solar heat and offering a dramatic view across a mean-
dering stream and into a sumptuous glen of dogwood trees. It was
completed in summer 1948 and its first occupants were Williams
and his wife, BMC student Vera Baker. 211
For the next few years Williams bounced between Black
Mountain and Boston, where he studied architecture at Harvard.
Along with the college’s first potter, Robert Turner, Williams
designed a concrete and wood pot shop, inaugurating an exciting
era of pottery at the college led by Turner, potter Karen Karnes
and her husband, potter and sculptor David Weinrib, and M. C. 2!2
In early 1952 Williams’s father died, leaving his son a nearly
$1 million inheritance. Williams decided to donate or loan much of
it to people and projects involved in art, architecture, and commu-
nity building. This included Black Mountain College, to which he
loaned $5,000 to build up a beef herd of 50 heifers, $5,000 for schol-
arship fees, and $5,000 for operational expenses. Williams also gave
$5,000 to John Cage, whom he had met at the college, to continue
his work with David Tudor on the Project for Magnetic Tape, which
began in New York and came with Cage when he taught at Black
Mountain College in the summer of 1952. 2'3
Williams's biggest gift to Black Mountain College was
also his last. In early 1953, he offered the college a $25,000 loan,
to be paid at $5,000 a year, interest-free. Sweetening an already
sweet deal, payment was not to begin until 1 September 1956. In
return, the college would offer the farm as collateral against the
loan. Dreier’s wartime decision to build up the farm as a strate-
gic capital investment was proving prescient. Once the deal was
signed, the college, which had been sitting at the precipice of
ruin, crawled along. 2'4

el.text: In June 1953, Olson, perhaps in a bid to secure future funding,
persuaded Williams to return to Black Mountain College, this time
to teach a course in architecture and serve as architect-in-residence.
Williams accepted and he, Vera, and their two young children trav-
eled to Black Mountain. They were shocked. As Davenport wrote,
“They quickly became alarmed with the school’s state of disarray,
the small number of students, and the lack of administrative leader-
ship.” No one, it seemed to Williams, was in charge. Before the end
of the 1953-54 school year, Williams and his family left the college
to establish an artists’ co-op, or intentional community, called the
Gate Hill Cooperative with former Black Mountain College faculty
and students including Cage, Karnes, M. C., experimental pianist
and composer David Tudor, Vanderbeek, and David Weinrib.?'5
While Doyle and Williams worked heroically to save Black
Mountain College, the real hero was the land itself. Although
the farm was nowhere near peak production, by 1953 it was still
providing the college with over half of the vegetables and fruit
BMCers ate and all of their meat, eggs, and butter. Lucky for the
current inhabitants, they were able to benefit from nearly two
decades’ worth of labor.
Black Mountain College began living off its land in a differ-
ent manner—namely, by selling it. Throughout the early 1950s, the
college enacted a series of entrepreneurial failures, each one worse
than the last. First, they sold off 70 acres of campus to a local gravel
company, who, as math student Trueman MacHenry recalled,
“engaged in scooping the heart out of the entire valley.” Upon selling
the parcel, the college learned they would have received the same
amount of money by merely leasing the land. Next, students Carl
Kent and Ron Robertson, under Doyle’s supervision, chopped and
trimmed pine trees from a stand near the farm hoping to sell the
lumber to local mills. Using only rudimentary axes they man-
aged to produce less than expected lumber and much more than
expected exhaustion. When additional funds produced two chain-
saws, the venture seemed viable. But soon one of the chainsaws
broke, and Kent and Robertson decided to leave the college and
return to New York, “stronger and healthier and also sadder because
we could sense we were seeing the last of a most significant and
wonderful learning community.” After that, writing student Fee
Dawson and painting student Jack Rice decided the college could
profit mightily by growing tobacco. With help from Doyle, they
planted acre after acre of the stuff. Next, they built a tobacco barn.
But these entrepreneurial students were inexperienced and built
the barn out of pine, a difficult wood to use in this capacity, mean-
ing construction lasted months longer than expected. Although the

and recently appointed interim farm manager, woke, rose, and left
his digs at two-story stone cottage Meadows Inn for early morning
milking duties on the farm. Within minutes housemate Michael
Rumaker rose, looked in on Terence’s room, winced at the color of
the sheets (“the shade of a good strong brew of coffee”), and tact-
fully closed the bedroom door, hoping to minimize the “barnyard
odor” that came from his housemate’s quarters. Rumaker woke

By late 1954, Black Mountain College was a precarious place—finan-
cially, functionally, spatially. To stay afloat, the college realized they
had to either lease or sell not just the land, as they had started doing,
but the campus itself. They entertained two or three offers and
eventually settled with George Pickering, a local businessman who

campus, which included the North and South Lodges, the largely

perhaps most importantly, the kitchen and dining hall. 222

its full-time cook in 1944. Since assuming that role, Malrey fed
the college grits and eggs, French toast with cinnamon, and piles
of pancakes for breakfast, soups and salads for lunch, and roasted
chicken and farm-fresh potatoes for dinner. She participated in
community meetings, taught students and an occasional faculty

THE FALL OF THE FARM
By fall 1954, farmer Doyle was fixing to leave Black Mountain
College. He felt betrayed by the college’s use of contingency salaries,
by which he received half of his salary (a measly $40) and an IOU
promising the other half when the college achieved financial stabil-
ity. He felt disrespected when the college offered to pay him some
of the IOU with food, including meat he raised and vegetables
he grew. He felt underappreciated, like the day when Doyle
slaughtered the farm’s remaining chickens, delivered them to cam-
pus, and watched as no faculty were willing to pluck them for din-
ner. Barbara Abrams, a student from New York, tried to pluck one
but instead threw up all over it. Eventually, Mary Fiore, who was
born in Ohio and arrived to the college on GI funding, stepped up
and plucked them all. When the campus community offered toasts
to celebrate the student who plucked the chickens, not the farmer
who raised them, Doyle felt sour. “The farmer felt he was doing
all the work, and the faculty was just sitting there eating his stuff,”
recalled Baker, “which it was.” 234
Making matters worse was Doyle’s relationship with Olson.
During the previous spring, Doyle and Olson were friendly. The
farmer invited the professor and his students to the farmhouse to
watch the Army-McCarthy hearings on Doyle’s television, the only
set on campus and the surrounding region. As a sign of apprecia-
tion, Olson and his students washed the windows of the farmhouse.
After that, however, something changed. Maybe it was because
Doyle did most of the farm work and Olson did none. Perhaps it
was their differing sizes—Olson, a giant, “King of the Mountain,”
Doyle, diminutive, “a short, leathery little man.” Whatever it was,
their “blood hatred” for one another climaxed in November 1954.
Fee Dawson witnessed it all: “I saw them pass in the hallway that
led from the kitchen to the back door of the dining hall; words
(animal) were exchanged; I followed Olson outside as he strode,
mind just able to control body, electrified with rage, and with
nowhere to go sat on the steps of North Lodge. Dan Rice was there.
Olson on the very brink opened and closed empty hands (around
Doyle’s neck), body shuddered, voice broke, snarled ‘I can’t FIGHT
that little bastard!” Shortly after that, Doyle had had enough. In
mid-November 1954, Doyle, “angry and sensing the end,” packed
up his family and belongings, including his television, and left
Black Mountain College for good. 285

in charge of the farm. Raised in Providence, Rhode Island, Burns

writing with Olson and painting with Joe Fiore. In place of tui-
tion he worked on the farm. “I was the milk boy,” Burns recalled.
“I used to milk a dozen milk cows twice a day.” 236

“It was a very meager scene.” For an entire quarter, student Barbara
Abrams ate cinnamon toast for breakfast, lunch, and dinner;
Carolyn Dunn heard of students surviving off “hot-dog soup,” pre-
pared by adding milk from the farm and herbs from the garden to
the water in which the hot dogs were boiled; and for a while, writ-
ing student John Wieners remembered being “penniless, living on
crackers and secondhand tea bags.” During the summer of 1955,
Wieners made an inventory of his food items that he hoped would
last him for one month; they included: “I quarter box of pancakes,
1 box of Hominy grits, % can of corn, 2 frankforts, and 20 crackers.”
Indeed, “people just sort of subsisted,” recalled Clemens Kalischer,
a photographer who visited campus in summer 1954, “I don’t know

Mountain College had to feed Olson. As Tom Clark noted, when

BURYING A COW
One night in December 1954, Black Mountain College’s 38 Hereford
cows disappeared. When acting farmer Terence Burns rose early
to milk the dairy cows, he discovered that the entire beef herd was
missing. While he was only in charge of the dozen dairy cows—
which provided the college with milk, cream, and occasionally some
subpar butter—the beef herd was under the domain of the Board of
Fellows, led by Olson. Certainly Olson talked like he was in charge
of the Herefords. “And here I was,” he was often heard saying after
becoming rector, “left with the total creation of 600 acres and 13
buildings, and windows and cows and stuff, roadways and every-
thing!” In letters and in conversations, he often referred to “my 38
Herefords.” Once, Olson boorishly compared himself to an enslaver.
“I used to watch my herd of Herefords,” he remarked, “like a great
plantation owner up there in the sun where we left them all spring,
from spring to fall.” While possessing grand visions, Olson possessed
neither skill nor interest in the cows. 246
Burns urgently woke up the college and a groggy motley
crew of professors—a patient Huss, a frantic Wolpe, a cranky Olson,
and an amused Landreau—was deputized to collect the college’s
cows. Some of the bovine escapees were lazy, made little ground,
and were quickly rounded up. Others were more ambitious, traveled
significant lengths, and were clearly a match for the wheezing fac-
ulty wranglers. “A sight to see, that was,” Landreau later recounted
in “The Cow,” a short story he wrote about the incident, “running
around out of breath, clumsy faculty members trying to chase cat-
tle.” The worst were the ones who had been lured into nearby farms.
When the panting professors asked their neighbors for their animals
back, the farmers, already suspicious of the city slickers and their
radical college, said, “What cows?” Only with intervention from a
local farmer and BMC friend did the farmers reluctantly give back
the escapees. By nightfall all of the college’s cows had been captured
and shoved into the school’s barn. This time, the barn door was
bolted shut. 247
A few days later Burns decided to check in with the cows.
He was aghast. Both the barn and the animals were a mess. The
barn was covered in a blanket of manure, with some stalls 3 ft deep
in it. The cows were hungry, swollen, and furious. The worst was
found in a stall at the back of the barn. There, an unfortunate cow
had slipped and drowned in its own shit. Not knowing what to do,
Burns consulted with faculty, who had zero ideas. Eventually Burns
called the friendly farmer, who called the local animal health inspec-
tor, who came to assess the situation, and ordered the college to dig
a hole at least 4 ft deep to “bury the poor creature.” Perhaps feeling
guilty for bringing the inspector’s rules into the rule-free college,
the friendly farmer stuck around and offered to clean the barn. 48
A team of nine was assembled to dig the internment. “It was
precisely New Year’s morning, 1955,” wrote Landreau, “light snow
falling on a small hillock behind the barn.” The ground was stony
and frozen. They struggled. It took hours. The only saving grace
was the jokes, mostly cow-related, told by the diggers, especially
Olson who, characteristically, talked more than he dug. Finally,
the inspector looked at the not-yet 4 ft deep hole and, taking pity,
declared it “deep enough.” Using the college’s tractor, the friendly
farmer unceremoniously hauled the dead cow from the barn into
its grave and the nine diggers shoveled dirt upon it. Someone,
probably Olson, offered a brief eulogy. 249

When class was over, Olson escorted the rep to the next class, taking
the longest possible route between two points. This gave students
enough time to change clothes and receive haircuts before their
next class, perhaps Huss’s drama class or Wolpe’s music class. And
so the day went: The VA rep was ushered through winding path-
ways between neck-high weeds to attend a new class with a differ-
ent professor who taught the same, albeit differently dressed and
groomed, students. As the VA rep left campus at the day’s end, the
remaining members of Black Mountain College celebrated their
theatrical success, a celebration that lasted until a few days later
when a letter arrived informing the college that their ineligibility
was upheld. Game over. 256

THE LAST DAYS OF
BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE
In summer 1956, as he was finishing his time in the army, Ebbe
Borregaard began to consider college. Raised in East Islip, Long
Island, by a creative family—his father was a vaudevillian-
turned-advertising man, his mother, a writer—Borregaard enjoyed
writing in high school. While stationed at Fort Eustis Army Base
in Newport News, Virginia, he wrote to Black Mountain College
to inquire about admissions. Unlike so many other letters to the
college, Borregaard’s was both opened and answered, by Eloise
Mixon. She included the faux brochure Olson had created for
the VA department. “It was a marvelous thing,” he recalled, “a list
of courses and how they were supposed to work.” Borregaard
packed his meager belongings, hitchhiked from Virginia to Black
Mountain, and arrived at the college in late September 1956. 25’
Although fall classes had not yet begun, Borregaard got
involved immediately with college activities. On his first full day he
accompanied some students to town where they taught him how
to steal food from the A&P. On his first night, he joined students
and faculty at Ma Peak’s. He enjoyed meeting his peers, despite the
constant hazing he received from two of them, Basil King and Eric
Weinberger, who peppered Borregaard with questions to determine
if he “was suitable enough for Black Mountain.” He participated
in multiple conversations about theater and attended the college’s
production of Medea, written and directed by Robert Duncan.
Because the cast included nearly the entire college community,
Borregaard was one of the few audience members. Compared to
his years in the army, BMC, with its utter lack of rules and regula-
tions, felt like freedom. “The place,” he remembered, “was such a
mind-blower.” 258
The place, Borregaard discovered, was also in ruins. “It was
overgrown,” he recalled, “and it was falling apart.” He made his way
to the library, which by then “had been ransacked,” and the Round
House, where he shuffled through the mostly melted records. It was
unclear to Borregaard where classes took place, where meals were
served, and where he would sleep. Worse, across campus there was
a stench, a smell of decomposition, “Everything smelled damp, like
damp wood, and moldy.” 259
On day five or six of Borregaard’s first—and only—week at
Black Mountain College, he, along with all other students, faculty,
and hangers-on, was summoned to Olson’s cottage. It was night-
time and Jalo House was lit with candles, since by then the electric-
ity had been turned off due to unpaid bills. Tea, most likely made

Black Mountain College, early October, 1956. Front (left to right): Eric Weinberger, Dan
Rice, Basil King, Betty Olson, Charles Olson, Harvey Frauenglass, Joe Fiore, Ebbe
Borregaard. Back (left to right): Wes Huss, unidentified man, Eloise Mixon, Don Mixon,

with recycled tea bags, was served. Eventually, Olson stood up and
announced: “The college is closing.” 260
Olson took in the shocked faces in the candlelit room.
“We need students,” he explained, most likely to a silent room full
of staring eyes. “We need paying students,” Olson clarified. The
students remained silent. “We can’t pay ourselves,” Olson went
on, adding with a poet’s precision: “We’ve got no money, no mon-
ey’s coming in, nobody’ll send us money.” One student and then
another offered to “write to grandma” to secure some money. With
a wave of his hand Olson dismissed such suggestions. “The college
is closing.” 261
Beer soon appeared and a low-key party began. Olson offered
a few fuzzy details. In order to pay off debts and contingency sal-
aries, the farm and upper campus would be sold. To prepare the
campus for sale, Olson would remain to clean up the place (an offer
that no doubt raised some unbelieving eyebrows). Huss shared his
plans to move to San Francisco to join Duncan and others to expand
Medea into a trilogy. Some discussed moving to New York; others
talked about relocating to Chicago. At some point, Dita Frauenglass,
who was married to writing student Harvey Frauenglass, took
a photograph and then another one, showing the last remaining
members of Black Mountain College, emaciated, drained, defeated.
As it got late, one by one the students and faculty returned to their
cottages. By night’s end, the college had closed. 262
The following day or perhaps the day after that, Borregaard
decided to join forces with the San Francisco crew. The idea was
to drive to California where they would connect with Duncan, his
partner and artist Jess, and BMC students and graduates like Paul
Alexander, Tom Field, Basil King, and Michael Rumaker, as well
as Beat figures like Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac, whose work
was featured in the seventh and final issue of The Black Mountain
Review. Borregaard packed his meager belongings, threw them
in the trunk, and jumped into the backseat of one of the cars head-
ing west. As they departed, he turned around to see Olson, on all
fours, frantically pulling weeds from the road that once led to Black
Mountain College. 263

David Silver’s fascinating study offers a new perspective of
the pioneering liberal arts school that was Black Mountain
College (BMC). Throughout the Depression and World
War II, the farm provided vital sustenance to the college’s
students and faculty while serving as a testing ground for
self-sufficiency, communal living, and collaboration—the
most precious ingredient at BMC.
The product of deep research, The Farm at Black Mountain
College follows renegade students, faculty, and farmers as
they establish a campus farm in the 1930s, build a better
farm in the 1940s, and watch it all collapse in the 1950s. We
meet a new cast of characters whose stories have seldom if
ever been explored, and whose adventures in agriculture
illuminate exactly what happened at the renowned college
across the decades: from optimistic community building
to its plunge into substance-addled scarcity.
